speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 30 the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska posed a question concerning the so-called refusal of the Canadian wheat board to sell July oats futures. I should like to give the answer to that question at this time.
The Canadian wheat board has not withdrawn offers to sell July oats futures. The board continues to offer, and sales are being made daily but in smaller volume due to limited availability. All stocks of oats in store at lakehead terminals have been
Inquiries of the Ministry contracted for, and the wheat board has ordered additional quantities forward from country elevators to meet commitments already entered into and to provide for additional sales contemplated under the July option. Stocks of oats in country elevators in western Canada are 9.4 million bushels.
In an effort to encourage increased producers' deliveries of this grain, a week ago the board authorized a supplementary quota on oats to 5 bushels per seeded acre with a minimum delivery privilege of 250 bushels per permit holder. Producers' deliveries to date this year have amounted to 27.7 million bushels compared with 15.3 million bushels to the same date a year ago.
The July oats futures opened on February 2, 1961 and the board has offered continuously in the market since that time and has sold a substantial volume for this delivery period. The initial sales were made at 77J cents per bushel, and there has been a small but steady increase in the futures market price since February 2, reflecting improved demand for available supplies.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DECREASE IN EXPORTS THROUGH PORT OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give an answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Levis concerning exportation of wheat from the port of Quebec.
The facilities at this port are used for both domestic and export movement of grain. During the last few years the volume of domestic business handled by this port has increased year by year, making up a large percentage of the port's business. In the fall the elevator contains large quantities of domestic grain and, consequently, smaller quantities of export grain. In the spring, when navigation opens, the facilities are busy replenishing stocks for domestic requirements.
Export clearances during the past few years have remained at about the same level of 9 per cent to 10 per cent in relation to total shipments from all St. Lawrence ports. This year this has been somewhat reduced owing largely to the domestic movement. However, as the year progresses and more grain is shipped from the lakehead to Quebec, I expect export clearances from this port to continue to increase and at the end of the crop season to reach close to the normal level of past experience.

The minister has given a very short and brief explanation of the items of which it is proposed to obtain approval in this measure now under discussion. It concerns the amount of, roughly speaking, $634 million broken up as you, Mr. Chairman, indicated to us a moment ago.
Before I enter upon the remarks which I intend to make I should just like to pose this question to the minister. Why has it been found necessary to ask for a two month's vote for interim supply? I ask the question anticipating that the reply of the minister will be that it is the usual and normal course to follow. However, the question which I am prepared to ask is this. Is it the usual course to follow when the estimates are under discussion as they have been under discussion during the course of the last several weeks

Interim, Supply
and, particularly, during the course of the period since morning sittings were initiated? As the minister knows, we have entered upon a discussion of the estimates of the various departments beginning on Wednesday, as a rule, and going right through, with but few exceptions, for the remaining days of the week. It therefore occurs to me that we should be given some explanation of this matter. Perhaps the minister, if he does not mind, will do so later.
Then there is another matter that comes to our minds at this time, namely that the minister has given little or no indication of his policy for the future, as I indicated on Saturday when I posed a question to the minister on the orders of the day inquiring when it was his intention to bring down the budget.
At that time I indicated to him that we were quite willing to co-operate in the passage of this measure for interim supply. However, I think it should be noted that cooperation is a two way street. Co-operation means co-operation not only from this side of the chamber but also from the government side as well. We are now into early June. The budget has not been presented, and this is a rather unusual situation. The new fiscal year started on April 1. Two months after entering upon the new fiscal year we do not know what the program of the government is; and by "program" I mean the outline of expenditures which the government has in mind. We know nothing of the money that will be required. We are in complete ignorance of the amount of the deficit which is envisaged by the government or the amount of money which will have to be borrowed by the government. We have no idea of the federal taxes which the Canadian people will be called upon to pay.
I think those various items which I have enumerated are matters about which the House of Commons and the Canadian people should know when we are discussing a measure of this importance. On Saturday the minister indicated that there was no direct relationship between the measure which would be discussed on Monday, namely this vote for interim supply, and the budget which he intends to bring down. I disagree with the minister. I think such is not the case. In my opinion there is not only an indirect but a direct relationship between the two matters. Normally the budget is brought down at the end of March or early in April. Last year it was brought down on March 31. I think it would be useful if the committee were to know the dates on which the budget has been introduced in this house in the last 17 or 18 years.

In 1946 the budget was presented on June 27. That was a late date, but having regard to the fact that the session was begun on March 14 it can easily be understood why the budget was not introduced much earlier. But that was an exceptional year. In 1947 it was introduced on April 29; in 1948, on May 18; in 1949, on March 22 and again on October 20; in 1950, on March 28; in 1951, on April 10; in 1952, on April 8; in 1953, on February 19; in 1954, on April 6; in 1955, on April 5; in 1956, on March 20; in 1957, on March 14; in 1958, on June 17; in 1959, on April 9; in 1960, on March 31 and December 20.
This gives some indication to the committee as to when the budget was introduced in the past. Here we are in early June and we have had no indication, contrary to what I believe are the rights of parliament, as to when the budget will be brought down.
The voting of supply is the traditional occasion for demanding the redress of grievances. It is the duty of the opposition to bring forward any grievances before voting supply. Here is a grievance now, a grievance of which we are complaining; that we on this side of the chamber, as well as the Canadian people, are entitled to know when the general presentation of the finances of the country is likely to be given to the house.
We are being asked to vote money before we know how these estimates are going to be spent. We are being asked to vote interim supply, but we do not know what the taxes are likely to be and what the whole expenditure program of the government is likely to be in connection with those very matters which we will be discussing.
It seems to me that the committee is entitled to a clear-cut statement by the Minister of Finance. We must know precisely when the budget will be brought down and whether there will be an appropriate and immediate opportunity for full debate. We do not want to be placed in the position we were put in last Christmas, when we had no opportunity to discuss the supplementary or baby budget, as it has been called. We were faced with an adjournment, and were not in a position to discuss it until several weeks later. I do not think we should be put in this position.
If the minister expects to obtain co-operation from this side of the chamber in connection with interim supply, he will get it; but as I indicated earlier, and I repeat it now, he will get it on certain conditions. He will get it on a condition which the opposition thinks it is entitled to obtain, and that is a clear statement by the minister of the matters about which I have asked, so that the opposition and all hon. members of the

house will be able to discuss the matters which normally come up in the budget, at the appropriate time.
If that were forthcoming I am sure the Minister of Finance and, for that matter, the government would certainly have no fault to find with the co-operation from this side of the chamber. That being so, I hope the minister will find it possible to respond to these questions which I have put to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Laurier first asks why the house is asked to vote two months' interim supply. The answer, which he himself has indicated is in his mind, is that this is the normal period for which interim supply is asked. This is a well established practice. In some years when the house was clearly on the eve of prorogation or the end of the session was in sight or two or three weeks away at the most it has sometimes not been necessary in the last interim supply motion to ask for more than one month. However, no one in this house I think would be bold enough to say he is absolutely positive that this session will end by June 30. So, Mr. Chairman, it is in keeping with the practice of the house and it is necessary under all the circumstances that the vote should be sought in the amount indicated.
As to the second point, Mr. Chairman, all I can say to the hon. gentleman is that the date for presentation of the budget has not yet been set. I am not in a position at the moment to announce the date. As soon as I am in a position to make the announcement I propose to do so. That has been the practice I have always followed in the past while I have held this portfolio, and the committee may be assured that the date will be communicated to the house in ample time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister what is the reason for this unusual delay in announcing the date of the budget?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I can agree with the hon. member that the delay is unusual. It must be remembered, in the first place, that this session has been unusual in that there has already been a budget. That budget was introduced in December; it was debated through January; a considerable number of measures arose out of it; the last of those measures only cleared this house several weeks ago, and one of them has not cleared the other place yet. So account must be taken of that fact in considering the date of this budget and comparing it with the dates of the budgets in other sessions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I should not wish to be held responsible for everything the hon. member for Essex East concludes from suggestions he has heard.
Mr. Chairman, will the minister give us a categorical assurance that there will be a budget in 1961?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have just said in reply to a question asked by the Acting Leader of the Opposition that I am hoping to bring down the budget before the end of this month.
That is not the question I asked. I asked the minister a simple question and I repeat it now. Will the minister give us a categorical assurance that there will be a budget in the calendar year 1961?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be my hope and expectation, Mr. Chairman.
I should like to ask the minister one more question. Does the minister expect that the budget will be brought down in sufficient time to permit the budget debate to take place in the month of June?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would depend on the date of the budget and on the arrangements that are made by the leader of the house and the whips of the parties, or those who have charge of these matters for the parties, as to the dates chosen for the debate.

In view of the fact that it is rumoured that the government intends that we shall adjourn at the end of June and come back either in August or in the fall, will the minister give us an assurance that if he does introduce his budget in the month of June-and from what he has now said it is not clear-there will be provided an opportunity of debating this most amazing budget in accordance with the practice laid down under our procedures allowing for six days of debate? While the minister is on his feet will he say whether his decision to postpone the introduction of the budget has something to do with the alarming state of the unemployment insurance fund and the suggestion that the deficit is likely to be not $700 million but closer to $1 billion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member will not be surprised when I tell him that I must reject categorically the

rumours and assertions that he heaped into the second part of his question.
In reply to the first part of the hon. member's question, let me say there has been no delay in the presentation of the budget, having regard to the fact that there was an earlier budget this year which ran its full course in this house and occupied, actually, rather longer than usual in being processed through all stages.
As to the dates of debate, that is again a matter for arrangement in accordance with the ordinary practice that prevails in the house. I should not think that the idea of a divided period would be acceptable to the house. I should think that when the house begins the budget debate it would probably wish to continue the debate until it has been concluded, but that must be a matter for discussion and arrangement among all parties in the usual course.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is one other matter on which I seek clarification, having to do with the statement the minister made earlier concerning the supplementary budget. I feel I should remind the minister that the supplementary budget of last December was supplementary to the budget of last year. It had nothing to do with this year's financial accounts. The other point which I think is of importance is one which I have raised indirectly earlier and which has now been raised more directly by the hon. member for Essex East. I refer to the opportunity to debate the budget when it is brought down.
We were placed in a most unusual position when the supplementary budget was brought down last December, in that we were not given an opportunity to discuss it until some weeks later. In other words, the budget was brought down in this house and the house adjourned-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. member not overlooking the opportunity provided for debate?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have not overlooked the opportunity provided to the financial critic of the opposition to make his remarks, but after all there are others in this house who are entitled to speak, and indeed the house generally is entitled to the opportunity to discuss the budget continuously without interruption so there can be an appropriate and full discussion of the financial accounts of the country.
The minister gave no affirmative answer this morning when we inquired whether an

opportunity for continuous uninterrupted debate would be provided. The minister said he hoped it would be possible for him to bring down the budget before the month of June is out. He went on to say he had every expectation that this would be the case. Let us suppose that the budget were introduced one day next week. This would mean that debate on the budget would not be entered upon until the following week. This would give an opportunity for six days of debate, as provided under our new rules, in the month of June. But suppose that were not the case and the introduction of the budget were delayed for another week. It would be impossible to discuss the budget continuously without interruption during the month of June.
While I realize we are not entitled to confidential information, on the other hand the opposition are entitled to know in connection with the matter now before us, interim supply, what is going to be the position of the government with respect to the discussion of the financial accounts of the country. The minister has gone some distance. He has said there will be no budget brought in this week. He went still further by saying that he hoped to introduce the budget this month. I believe we are entitled to know whether, in bringing down the budget this month, there will be an opportunity for continuous discussion of the budget before the month is out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think I can usefully add anything to what I have said. The days set aside for debate on the budget will have to be arranged in the usual course. It is the house leader who makes those arrangements, not the minister introducing the budget. I think the views of hon. members opposite are known in this regard. I am sure that in whatever arrangements are made, effort will be exerted to make such arrangements as will accommodate the wishes of the house. I do not know what more I can say.
The request for interim supply that is made this morning makes provision for only the months of June and July, so that if the business of the house were not finished before July and if there were to be some adjournment proposed at that point, there would have to be a request made for a further vote of interim supply. The rights of the house are fully protected in that regard.

There is one aspect of this problem I think we should emphasize. We have been discussing, and I believe justifiably, the rights and convenience of hon. members of this house with regard to an opportunity to discuss the budget which the minister now assures us is going to be 90205-6-370J

brought in some time in the course of the present calendar year. We hope this will be done before the end of June.
We must also consider, however, the question of public convenience. The minister says the delay in the introduction of the budget does not present an unusual picture in the sense that a delay of this kind has occurred before, although he has not satisfied me that there has been a parallel situation since confederation. The fact that there was a baby budget in December does not in any material way affect the fact that the budget normally presented before this time has been unduly delayed. The effect of this delay, as my hon. friend knows better than anyone else, is being felt throughout the country at a time when there should be definite knowledge on the part of business, industry, agriculture and the work community as to the intentions of the government, so all these groups can make the preparations they have to make in regard to their operations, including the kind of adjustments which inevitably flow from the presentation of a budget.
We are entitled to know from the minister at this stage, not what his budgetary proposals are, but the explanations for this delay. We are not receiving them from the Minister of Finance. We have been directing questions to the minister since Easter as to when the budget was going to be brought down, yet none of his replies at any time suggested that we should not expect the budget until some time well into the month of June at the earliest. Because of the fact that the minister at one time gave the impression that he was ready to present the budget-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I never gave that impression.
Well then, because of the fact that, in my judgment, he left that impression, and his words are there to be seen-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.
He has certainly given the impression that he was ready. That has now been changed, and I cannot-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. gentleman to point out my words to which he has reference?
I am afraid I cannot at this time, but in all fairness to the hon. gentleman I will ascertain those words which gave me this impression. Perhaps some of my colleagues will find them in the meantime.

In any event that was my impression. That hon. gentleman who always comes to the assistance of the Minister of Finance has said that I will never find them. Perhaps he can offer some explanation in this regard.
All I am seeking to say now is that the Minister of Finance cannot take the position that he is going to hold the country in suspense beyond a reasonable period, and he should give us some definite reasons for this change. I have asked him two questions which he has treated lightly. I asked him first whether the delay in presenting the budget is because the deficit is going to be even more glaring than that suggested by the tax foundation and certainly much in excess of what the minister himself forecast last year. I then asked the minister if the delay was caused because of his wish to avoid the embarrassment which will come because of the state of the unemployment insurance fund. If those are the reasons they are legitimate, particularly the latter. The minister could tell us whether he intends to ,bring in legislation to replenish that fund, there now being no authority to make loans to the fund under the Unemployment Insurance Act because there are no securities which can be pledged in sufficient amounts. This again reflects the serious state-
There are.

There are not enough securities in the fund now to warrant the Minister of Finance making loans which would put the fund into a condition of security and give the necessary confidence to those who have contractual rights under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The minister may nod his head, but if that is the situation-that there has been a sudden burst in unemployment insurance revenues, I should like to remind him that seeding is now under way, businesses are even now getting ready for their autumn work, and there is a serious stagnation confronting the automobile industry.
I asked the Minister of Finance the other day whether, in view of the decline of over 10.45 per cent in production of commercial and other motor vehicles, he could say that he was prepared to give some relief. Mr. Speaker said at that time that under our rules I had no right to anticipate questions of that kind involved in the budget. Surely in the face of this kind of situation it is not unfair to ask the minister when he is going to bring down his budget so that industry, among others, will know what the situation is. Those are not unfair questions, I suggest.
The report of the royal commission under the direction of Professor Bladen was given

the Prime Minister five or six weeks ago. The government has had an opportunity of examining that report. If it has not taken that opportunity then it is certainly remiss in the performance of its obligations. I recognize how busy the ministers are, particularly the Minister of Finance, but I have no doubt that he has had that report carefully examined, and if it has no relation whatsoever to the budget it ought to be tabled so we can ascertain the situation from the point of view of the commissioner in order that we may determine what course to take during the budget debate. If the minister informs us that he cannot reveal the contents of that report because it is to play a very important part in his budget and, as a result, he has not been able to do the necessary homework, even though his statement might not be approved it would be understood. However, those are considerations which the Minister of Finance ought to explain to this house. I do not know under what prerogative the Minister of Finance takes the position that he does not have to give a more definitive accounting to the house with regard to the presentation of the budget. No minister of finance is a law unto himself, no matter how much of a law unto himself he may be in the cabinet.
Oh, oh.

The Minister of Finance laughs and I laugh back at him, because no matter how much of a law he may be in the cabinet, that is not his position in this parliament, nor is it his position in the country; and the Canadian people have a right to know why this postponing and procrastinating government has delayed so long in presenting its financial accounts to the nation. I suggest to the minister that this is a bit of finessing; that in the absence of a positive reason the minister is hoping to be able to divert public attention from the financial situation which has evolved under this government. If it is a fact that we are going to have a deficit of over $700 million, let alone a deficit of $1 billion, it is understandable that the minister is seeking to coincide our initial discussion on the budget with an adjournment so that the dreadful news may, on that account, be received with less objection on the part of the Canadian people.
If those are not the reasons for this delay the Minister of Finance should stop this humourous appreciation of a serious argument and tell us exactly why the budget is not being presented. The Minister of Finance may laugh, but I should like to tell him-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot help it.

-that the people in the country who are out of work, and the businessmen of this country facing these conditions of stagnation as a result of the financial policies of this government are not going to laugh. They will be greatly amused today by the reactions which the Minister of Finance has displayed toward suggestions that have come from us in the Liberal party when we have asked reasonable questions of the minister.
Why does the minister not now tell us that the reason he has not brought down the budget is that he is not ready and that certain considerations have yet to be given? If that is the situation I suggest we are entitled to know what those considerations are, unless they go to the very root of the secrecy of the budget itself.
I suddenly recall, and would remind the minister, what happened in the British house with regard to the repeal of certain laws having to do with maize, when a situation arose not unlike the present situation. When the chancellor of the exchequer, Mr. Ritchie, was asked to state when he intended to bring down his budget he refused and sat mute in his seat, like the Minister of Finance, and possibly arrogant, like the Minister of Finance. It was that arrogance which caused the government of which Mr. Ritchie was a member to lose its life and its head when the next election took place. That, of course, is what is going to happen to this government.
What about the byelections?

And one of the
main contributors toward the fall of the head of the government will be the serene, unimpassioned, unexcited Minister of Finance who sits in his seat so quietly and serenely on Monday, June 5, 1961.

Mr. Chairman, as we move into committee of supply today we must realize, of course, that there are many problems facing this government, and I am sure they would be the last ones to deny it. In addition I believe also many problems are facing the people of this country which they are given to believe the government is not aware of. We have signs of squalor, and unemployment. There are problems connected with defence, transport, external affairs, and so forth. We must also realize that some of the estimates of departments we shall deal with today have already passed through this house. They have been subject to detailed discussion. We hope that the other departments will soon be before the house and again their estimates will be subjected to detailed
Interim Supply
discussion. In fact, notwithstanding the fencing and political footwork that we have witnessed here this morning, we may even hope that, since the by-elections have been held, we shall have a budget before us one of these days.
Therefore it is not my intention to cover the waterfront in this debate. I should like to discuss one problem only, namely the position in which the old age pensioners find themselves today. The problem of the old age pensioners is unique. If we look at the other problems we find that the sick can possibly look forward to getting well and the unemployed can look forward to the possibility of a job in the future if things take an upturn. If they do not, they can hope at least to hang on until the next election, when they will be able to take some positive action. International tensions can improve, and we all hope they will. But if all these problems were solved it would still leave the old age pensioners in the same position they are in at the present time.
What is ahead for our old age pensioners? Only one of two things can happen to them in which they find themselves at the present time. The first is to lower the cost of living. The second is to raise the old age pension. Either solution can help the old age pensioners today. Unfortunately this government has raised rather than lowered the cost of living since it took office. We see no signs of any change in this regard at the present time This government has not raised the old age pension, although its promise to do so is now four years old.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We did raise it in 1957.
Yes, but that was tour years ago. At the time it was raised there was a clear promise that it was only a temporary measure and the amount would be raised in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.
This idea was sold to the Canadian public and the old age pensioners of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That just is not true.

This government has raised the veterans disability pension during this session. That was a commendable move which received the full support of the house. In more recent days the government have also raised the war veterans allowance. I believe they raised it even higher than the amount asked for by the legion. This again is very commendable and received the full support of the house, but the position of

Mr. Chairman, I want to put on the record something to which I alluded when I spoke last. I said the minister did give me the impression during the course of this session that he had just about finished the necessary preliminaries which would enable him to bring in his budget. I now want to put on the record my support for that position. On March 29, as will be found at page 3461 of Hansard, the hon. member for Wellington South put this question to the Minister of Finance. I think it is significant that the question was put by a member on the government side. While I have the highest regard for the hon. member for Wellington South, I am sure he will not misunderstand me if I say he has not taken part too often in questions on the orders of the day, and one may reasonably conclude that this was a planted question, in other words a question which he asked at the insistence of the Minister of Finance. This is the question the hon. member asked:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Will the minister indicate to the house whether he has yet established a deadline date by which time he hopes to complete hearing delegations making representations in respect of the main budget?
The Minister of Finance replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I hope to complete the hearing of the delegations by the end of next week, April 8.
Now, everyone knows that once a minister of finance has completed hearing delegations he is then in a position to put the finishing touches on his budget-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

-and get the
necessary consent of his cabinet colleagues. My hon. friend says "No". I am speaking

from some experience over a long time in government, and I am sure this government's experience is no richer than that of other governments. In any event, on March 29 the Minister of Finance said he hoped that the hearing of delegations would be over by April 8. This is the reason I clearly had the impression that the minister would then be ready to present his budget shortly afterward. Something has intervened in the meantime and we are entitled to know, I repeat, why the Minister of Finance is now, on the 5th day of June, unable to give the hon. member for Laurier, who put this question on behalf of the opposition, the kind of reply which would normally be given by any other minister of finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am indebted to the hon. member for Essex East for exposing to the committee the manner in which he misled himself into the state of mind which he indicated earlier in his remarks. What I said on March 29, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Wellington South, was that I hoped to complete the hearing of the delegations making representations in regard to the budget "by the end of the next week, April 8". The hon. member has been out of office for four years, Mr. Chairman, and he must have forgotten that normally after the completion of the hearing of delegations there is a great deal of work to be done on the budget. In my experience the hearing of the delegations for a budget brought in in April was completed about the end of January, and it is quite customary for about two to two and half months, in that range of time, to pass after the hearing of the delegations is completed before the budget is introduced in the house.
In the four years that he has been out of office the hon. member has forgotten that a tremendous amount of work has to be done after the completion of the hearing of the delegations. That is one of the earlier stages in the work of preparing the budget. So if he will add two and a half months to the date referred to for completion of the hearings he will find that we are running about on schedule. I might also remind him that the earlier period this year, when in a normal year the hearing of the delegations would have been done, was devoted as far as the Minister of Finance was concerned to sitting in the house following the debate on the budget and on the measures arising out of the budget.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance has given an explanation of his procedure in preparing the budget. I suppose that precisely how he conducts himself in preparing the budget is not the concern of

the house, but I would not want the impression to go across the country that over the years successive finance ministers have stopped hearing delegations two and a half months before the presentation of the budget. They have heard delegations right up to the last week before the presentation of the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.

The minister says that is not correct. I do not want to use language that you would rule out of order, Mr. Chairman, but may I say that many delegations have presented their representations on major financial matters as little as a week or ten days before the actual delivery of the budget. I have every reason to believe that the representations of those delegations were treated with respect and decisions were taken on them after they had been considered thoroughly by the finance minister of the day.
I can only draw the conclusion that the Minister of Finance has somehow revealed a situation that is a cause for concern in the country, in that the machinery for considering representations and taking decisions thereon on the part of the government is not adequate to the task. The reason for that will remain something peculiarly within the knowledge of the government and a few people working closely with it, but there is some alarming breakdown in the machinery, and what it is we have a right to know.
When the Minister of Finance brushes aside requests for information as to the date of the delivery of the budget and the other representations of my colleagues on this matter of such great concern to the Canadian public, he forgets that in part the great concern over the failure to deliver the budget stems from a certain action on his part for which he must remain answerable. I remind him that he is the Minister of Finance who in the previous parliament, between the 1957 and 1958 elections, refused to deliver a budget as such. He was the new Minister of Finance of a new government taking office after 22 years in opposition who refused to make known the state of the public accounts to the people of this country during the whole life of that parliament. He is the one who refused to state what changes in fiscal policy the new government proposed.
I said at the time in the house and I repeat now that that failure caused a great deal of doubt and hesitation in the business community of this country. It has done more than that. It has been a contributing factor in the slowing down of business activity in the last few years. However much the minister may defend his action' on that occasion, I remind

him now that it does leave him in the position of being suspect when we recall that the house has been meeting since last November and, having in mind the length of the session, it could reasonably have been expected that the budget would be delivered in April. With that background on his part, whether he was right or wrong in doing so, the delay and the unsatisfactory explanations for such delay have created a situation in the country that is most damaging to the economy.
I would hope that he would see fit to answer fully as best he can, so that the businessmen of the country who are concerned with the budget and the public generally will know when they may reasonably expect the budget to be delivered, the precise reasons for the delay, and will also be given the related information of a nature that can properly be given and does not entrench upon any of the matters with relation to the contents of the budget itself which must by their nature be kept secret. I should like to ask the minister a question. He referred to the fact that we have already had a budget this year and he was referring, of course, to the baby budget. This morning is the first time I have ever heard him call it a budget. It was not a statement of the government accounts. The only figures he brought before the house had to do with a surplus or a deficit. In the previous budget he had forecast a surplus of $12 million and in December he came along and said there would be a deficit of $286 million. These are the only figures he brought forward. They had nothing to do with the government accounts. I should like to ask the minister whether he considers that is a proper accounting to parliament and the people with respect to the government accounts.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take a few minutes to express my personal concern that thus far we not only have no budget but we have no indication when it is going to be presented. My particular concern is as to any announcements that may be made by the Minister of Finance with relation to our Canadian financial structure from the point of view of trade. I know that we have already dealt with the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but there have been developments since that time which I am certain must be of concern to the government and particularly to the Minister of Finance; therefore there may be something in the budget that will deal with this most important phase of our economy.
I also cannot help wondering whether the delay in bringing down the budget, which of course is a policy statement, may be having a detrimental effect on our export trade in that some of our industries and manufacturers may be refraining from pursuing an aggressive policy trying to sell Canadian goods abroad. Only last week I noted in a Vancouver newspaper the statement by an official of the timber industry that our export sales in the previous month were down 2 per cent. That is a very important matter to the province of British Columbia at this time of the year.
I also could not help but note and feel disturbed, as I hope the government is, about a statement which appeared in one of the eastern newspapers just a matter of two or three weeks ago. Mr. Victor G. Bailey, Jamaican publisher of the Caribbean Spotlight magazine, stated that Canada is rapidly losing its position as a traditional supplier in the West Indies market. He stated that the main reason is Canada's lack of a go-getting sales approach. On the occasion of this speech or interview he gave some most startling facts. Not only did he point out that we were rapidly losing out on our traditional West Indies market, but that we were losing out on the importation by the West Indies of those goods for which Canada is, I would say, an absolute natural. He says that West Germany, Japan and Italy are flooding the West Indies market with precisely the kind of products made by Canadian factories. For example, West Germany sold 11,526 radio sets in Jamaica and Japan sold 2,627, while Canada sold only 35. That is one illustration. But may I come to a product which is an absolute natural. Here is what we find in a statement made by Mr. Victor G. Bailey:
Even in items which the West Indies thought synonymous with Canada, he said, newcomers to the market are pushing out Canadians.
Holland, said Mr, Bailey, sold 343,125 pounds of paper bags in the West Indies while Canada sold

21,654 pounds; and West Germany supplied 216,870 hundredweight of counter flour, compared with only 10,983 hundredweight from Canada.
The situation is getting fairly serious when in an attractive West Indies market, in matters of wheat, counter flour, and products made from our timber resources such as paper bags, we are being completely wiped out by other countries, according to this information. It is something new.
In view of this report of what is happening and in view of the information I gave a few moments ago with regard to declining exports of our forest products from British Columbia at this time of the year, I say this is something that cannot be ignored by this House of Commons or by the Minister of Finance. I would expect the budget to contain something of a policy nature. I say it is bad for Canada and for parliamentary procedure that we should not have had a budget by this time. To my mind it is almost tantamount to a dereliction of duty, a lack of concern for the well-being and welfare of Canada.
As emphatically as possible I want to say that although we cannot do anything about the past, I sincerely hope that just as speedily as possible or almost immediately the budget may be brought down, and that it may have in it some policy analysis and statement and some forward looking views and recommendations to deal with the many problems which are of concern to our people, and the many factors which we see developing and which can be a hindrance to the economy of Canada.
A grave responsibility rests upon the Minister of Finance. Although we can hardly find words with which to condemn his lack of action or his lack of speed in the past, we sincerely hope he will now give us some indication that the government is concerned about what is taking place and that there will be almost immediately an explanation to this House of Commons and to the Canadian people of the fiscal and economic policies of this government. I would say this is a necessity for, let alone a demand by the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have another question I should like to direct to the minister. Before doing so, however, I think I should commend the attitude taken by the hon. member for Vancouver East, which was entirely opposed to that of the hon. member for Timmins. The hon. member for Timmins seemed to think that we were simply shadow-boxing with the minister from this side of the house on a matter of perhaps little or no consequence. However, the hon. member for Vancouver East has in effect, I believe, rebuked the hon. member for Timmins, who did not seem to

think that the rights of parliament were affected in any way in this matter. We on this side of the house say they are affected. We repeat what has already been said, namely, that there is a direct relationship, to say nothing of an indirect one, between what is being asked at the moment, namely supply to the extent of $634 million, and the bringing down of the budget itself.
However, what I rose to deal with was a matter which the minister has already put on record in connection with the question which was put to him by the hon. member for Wellington South on March 29. In explaining away that question the minister used these words: "A great deal of work must be done after the representations in respect of the main budget have been made". I presume no one will find fault with this statement by the minister. However, the true story is that a great deal of work is done prior to that time. A great deal of work is done by the experts in the Department of Finance in preparation for the budget. The minister said on March 29, as found at page 3461 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I hope to complete the hearing of the delegations by the end of next week, April 8.
When he said that surely he had not in mind that this important work would not be completed until after June 10th. On Saturday he indicated that the budget would not be brought down this week. The only conclusion to which I can come is that between the time this statement was made and the time the budget will be brought down something has happened to estop the minister; to make him change his opinion or to make him consider other amendments than those which he intended to bring down.
I am not complaining about the fact that it is necessary to do all these things. What I am complaining about, and what I think everyone in this house has a right to complain about, is the fact that it has taken more than two months for those representations of which the minister has spoken to be implemented in the form of an actual presentation. There is no doubt in my mind that this was a planted question. I do not mean to be disrecpectful to the hon. member or to anyone else. Here the answer was clear:
Mr. Speaker, I hope to complete the hearing of the delegations by the end of next week, April 8.
Here we are at June 5, approximately two months later, and thus far we have had no indication of when the budget will be brought down. We have from the minister a statement of hope and expectation. There is hope and expectation on the part of the minister that the budget will be brought down before the end of the month. I do not think that is sufficient. I think the minister should make a

definite statement, yes or no; and I think he can do that without divulging any information that should not be given to the house. I think he should tell us categorically whether or not we are going to get the budget before the month is out. In view of what was stated here in the month of March I think the committee is entitled to know what the position is with reference to the financial accounts of the country at this late date.
Shall the resolution carry?
Carried.
Is the minister not going to answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I answered the same questions earlier this morning, and there is nothing I can add. Perhaps the minister has given us the explanation now. He says "There is nothing I can add". That is no doubt the explanation of why we have not had the budget; he has got nothing to add. The treasury is empty; he does not know what his deficit is going to be.

Mr. Chairman, this is the second time this session the Minister of Finance has come before the committee for interim supply. I do not think it is out of order for him to ask for interim supply for two months, one sixth of the estimates. I think that is O.K. Ever since I have been in the house, when asking for interim supply the government has always asked for one sixth of the estimates.
In voting interim supply hon. members of this committee have an opportunity and a right to raise grievances. On this side of the chamber we believe that the matters we wish to put before the committee could more properly be raised in a budget debate. In fact we will cut down our discussion on interim supply to the minimum and do all we can to process it through the different stages of the house.

Interim Supply
The minister referred this morning to the baby budget. That certainly was not in any way, shape or form an accounting to this country. The only accounting the minister gave was that he would have a big deficit instead of a small surplus. There was no accounting for any one government account.
I do not think our request is unreasonable. It is almost two months since the completion of the last fiscal year, and we are voting money day after day in the estimates. We are voting millions of dollars, and we have not a clue whether or not we are going to have the money. We have no idea how much money will have to be borrowed. I think the minister could probably give us that information now, but he refuses to do so.
Never before in the history of parliament has the session lasted for so long without an accounting to parliament by the Minister of Finance. This session started in November and is now over seven months old. It is true that in two or three election years-and I have gone away back in looking at this matter-and in one war year the budget was presented as late as the latter part of June, but in those particular years the session started either in March or April.
When the minister presented his last June budget I have forgotten the date parliament was called back after the election in 1958, but it was very late, and he presented his budget rather early in the session. If the minister would give us the assurance now that he will bring down the budget some time this month and give us an opportunity to debate it, we on this side of the chamber will not pursue the matter further.
However, I feel that if the minister will not give this assurance I should raise those matters which I should like to put before the committee at this time. I will say this; if the minister is not able to give this assurance to the committee we can only conclude, and the country can only conclude, that he has not the intestinal fortitude to put the financial position of this country before the people.
That is right.

As I have said before, a year ago the minister predicted a surplus of $12 million and at the end of the year, in December, he predicted a deficit of $286 million. I predicted then that he would never have a surplus. I predicted three years ago that the Minister of Finance would never have a surplus. I hope his figure of $286 million is right. I predicted it would be more and I hope, for the sake of the taxpayers of Canada, that my prediction is wrong.
They all are.

I have read different references in the press. I saw one in a Montreal newspaper the other day to the effect that our deficit for the last fiscal year would be between $700 million and $1 billion. I say that when the government refuses to give an accounting to parliament the Prime Minister and the government are holding parliament in contempt; they are taking away some of the rights of parliament from its members. How can we carry on and discharge our duties in a proper way unless we have the fundamental information with which to carry on parliament? After all, the author of the Canadian Bill of Rights, the Prime Minister, is taking rights away from the members of this house.
I read in the current press that the Minister of Finance created a pitiful and sad spectacle when trying to get the chartered banks to reduce the interest rate at the same time as the governor of the Bank of Canada was doing nothing in that regard. Surely this is a matter for discussion. It is time the minister laid his cards on the table. The minister has refused to bring the governor of the Bank of Canada before a committee of this house. We should have an opportunity to question the governor.
The report of the Bank of Canada says nothing about salaries, and I think we should have an opportunity to question the governor about salaries. I am not particularly interested in the salary that any one particular person receives, but I do think we should know what the total salaries are. We should also know something about the building of premises. I have heard-I do not know whether it is true -that the Bank of Canada builds and rents premises. From my reading of the Bank of Canada Act I think the bank has no right to build and rent premises.
I have said before that there is no room in Canada for two sovereignties. The government should take responsibility for fiscal policy, but so far they have taken no responsibility in this respect. The Minister of Finance has said that the governor of the Bank of Canada is responsible only to parliament. Then why does he not call the governor before a committee of this house so we may question him? The governor of the Bank of Canada has said on two occasions that he has a cure for Canada's ills. He has said he knows how to cure unemployment. Evidently the government is not following the recommendations of the governor, or hon. gentlemen opposite would have introduced a solution to the unemployment problem. The governor should appear before a committee of this house in order that we may question him on these points.

The Canadian economy is sick. This is not the time to introduce a budget designed to

The minister made reference to the baby budget. The only thing of much moment in that budget was the half hearted, wishy washy measure to assist depressed areas. Not long ago there was only one so-called depressed area, and today we elicited information to the effect that two or three other communities have qualified for assistance under this plan. I doubt whether one man has been put to work under this program since the measure was introduced. The government had every right to proceed under this program after it was announced in the baby budget last December.
If we had the right kind of leadership our economy could be reinvigorated and we could get going again. If proper action were taken the unemployment insurance fund would look after itself because there would be more employment. The United States economy is building up, but if one reads the Financial Post one learns that after a slight pick-up the Canadian economy is again faltering. We need assistance from this government to stimulate our economy and assist the business community.
Last year business failures in Canada were at the highest level since the Tory thirties. There is no doubt about that. Immigration has gone down to a trickle, and according to recent press reports more people are leaving Canada today than are entering the country. It is true that our population is increasing because of the increased birth rate, but at the present time more people are leaving Canada than are taking up residence here. Taxes are higher now than ever before at all levels of government. People are going hungry in our cities, including the minister's home city of Toronto. Unemployment is higher in Canada than in any other country in the western free world. A recent article in the New York Times indicated that our unemployment level is approximate two and one half percentage points higher than that of Italy, the next worst country in that respect in the western free world. Our federal bonds have sold at prices lower than the bonds of cities elsewhere including the cities of Hamburg, Buenos Aires and Oslo.
I have been right in a good many of my predictions. I venture to predict now that if we have another four years of federal fiscal

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I said that this government needed leadership. I should like to emphasize that statement at this time by saying that this country needs leadership now. Before we adjourned at one o'clock I intended to deal more with the program of action as described in the Victoria Colonist, in an advertisement paid for by the Progressive Conservative party. There appears in this advertisement, among other things, the following statement:
When this government entered office in 1957 immediate action was required and was taken- a serious recession was under way-these measures were taken-
Following1 that statement there appears a list of 12 measures, and I should like to refer to No. 10, which is as follows:
10. $500 million aid to Canadian shipbuilding industry.
In this house we voted a $1 item in the estimates of the Department of Transport.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
There was a $1 item included there.
It was just promised, not voted. It was just another promise.
That is right.
The minister should look at page 4784 he will find there the Minister of Transport's promise.
Who has the floor?

I suggest we have been kept in the dark in regard to this $500 million program. I should like the minister to tell us what was intended by the inclusion of that $1 item in the estimates of the Department of Transport, as well as this program involving $500 million as indicated in the advertisement of the Progressive Conservative party.
I suggest that information was made public in that way as election bait, and that the elected members of this house were given

indication only of the $1 item. I wonder whether the minister can tell us why we are being asked to vote that $1 item in view of the announced plan regarding the $500 million in aid to the shipbuilding industry. At the same time I would ask the Prime Minister what has happened to the bill of rights in this regard.
It is no wonder that in this country we are in such a financial mess, and no wonder that the government has had to ask the taxpayers of Canada to foot the bill for $800 million in extra interest over a four year period. The trouble resulted from this government's policy, commenced at the time of the baby budget in December of 1957, followed by the losses suffered by the conversion loans, in turn followed by the high interest on borrowings which this country has had to make.
I should like at this time to briefly refer to the 1960 income tax rate. Many individuals have been fooled this year in regard to their 1960 income tax return because this government has raised the rate paid by individual taxpayers. In 1959 individual taxpayers paid the increase for that year from July 1 on, but in 1960 they had to pay the increased rate for the whole year. Many individuals have asked me why that is so. I suggest the reason is that the government has raised the income tax while at the same time it has lead people to believe that it has lowered it. I suggest this situation has become fully known to the individual taxpayers following their filing of returns for 1960.
The minister referred to the fact that he presented the baby budget to this house at a period when I was absent because of illness.
I should like to inform him that at the particular time it was presented I was overseas in the company of other hon. members of this house attending a NATO parliamentary conference. I was at the officers' mess of one of the fighter wings in France when the news of the baby budget arrived from Paris.
I felt it was bad news at the time, and was asked to comment in respect to it. I said at the time I felt it would not in any way help our economy and that it bore out my prediction that the $12 million surplus, which the minister had forecast, would in fact turn out to be a huge deficit.
I am sure all hon. members have read press reports regarding the financial difficulties suffered by Britain at different times, particularly following the wars. The government of that country, as well as the chancellor of the exchequer, has always been able to step into the breach by adopting measures to improve the situation. I wish that we had a

government in Canada that would step into the breach in order to cure our ills at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to be very brief in my remarks this afternoon. At the outset I must say that our group has been restrained because of our impression that the members of this committee were going to all restrain themselves at this time in order to facilitate the business at hand. I suggest that we have kept our word in that regard.
Before proceeding with the matter in respect of which I rise at this time, I should like briefly to support the representations made by the hon. member for Timmins. I refer to his plea to the government for consideration of the plight of many of the persons in receipt of old age security and old age assistance payments. As we see it we have a responsibility to our senior citizens to make sure that they are able to enjoy their declining years with at least a measure of comfort and some security.
In order to save the time of the committee I will not go further in that direction. I rose particularly to proceed with a question that I raised on the estimates of the Secretary of State last Saturday. I was ruled out of order because the person I wished to deal with is a public servant and not a civil servant as I was informed. Therefore I trust that this afternoon I am completely in order.
First of all I wish to refer briefly to two or three news reports which have caused us, and I think a number of people in Canada, some concern. The first is a report in the Gazette of Saturday, June 3, which reads:
Chaput says he'll reply In few days
Dr. Marcel Chaput, vice president of a Quebec secessionist movement, yesterday said he will reply within a few days to an invitation that he quit his defence research job.
He said he will issue a statement replying to Dr. J. E. Keyston, vice president of the board. Dr. Keyston said Thursday Dr. Chaput's "political activities" are incompatible with his work as a federal government civil servant.
First of all, I must say we think it is highly improper for the vice-chairman of the defence research board to make a public statement to the press with respect to Dr. Chaput. I am quite sure he has started something that is bound to end up in Dr. Chaput getting justice from all quarters. I understand that Dr. Chaput addressed an independence meeting recently and said that "Quebec will secede from confederation before 1967 if the secessionist movement continues to expand at the present rate". Of course there is a big "if" there. A number of people have asked me the meaning of the word "secede". I understand it is to go apart, to leave, or to
Interim Supply
assume a different unit or grouping, and so on. Then in the Gazette of Monday, June 5, I read:
Chaput still backs secessionist group refuses to quit Ottawa job.
Speaking in French, he said:
"In the dispute between myself and my employer, there is, as far as I'm concerned, only one possible reply: I have no intention of resigning from the defence research board Or from the vice presidency of the R.I.N."
This was his reply to an invitation from the board that he resign.
Dr. J. E. Keyston, vice chairman of the board, said last week he considers it "morally and ethically inconsistent that anyone should publicly urge the disruption of the federal government while continuing to be employed by the government."
First of all, I think comment on the action of an employee of this status is the responsibility of the minister and not that of the vicechairman of the board. I think the vice-chairman of the board should know better than to make such press statements. Because of this unfortunate publicity a certain amount of understandable resentment and concern has been aroused in certain quarters. In this morning's Gazette I read:
Dr. Chaput supported in Ottawa.
This reaction is the result of precipitate and unfortunate publicity on the part of the vice-chairman of the defence research board. The article goes on:
Five French language Canadians have formed a "civil rights committee", a group to back up financially any French language Canadians restrained in the exercise of their civil rights.
The five men are Gaetan Legault, an Ottawa lawyer; Claude Trottier, a Quebec city industrialist; Pierre Laporte, a Montreal newspaperman; Paul-Emile Robert, a Montreal life insurance underwriter, and Jacques J. Paris, a Hull translator.
Formation of the group was decided during the week end following the suggestion that Dr. Marcel Chaput resign his defence research board job because of "political activities".
Later on in the report we find:
"We are not separatists," said the five men in a statement. "But we believe that any French Canadian patriot threatened, because of his opinion, in the exercise of his civil rights deserves the moral support and the financial backing of all his compatriots."
We agree with this statement. We are concerned about this unfortunate situation and publicity on two grounds. First, we are concerned with freedom of speech, the right of free association and the right to political opinions being enjoyed by public servants. We believe in the system they have in Great Britain where those civil servants who have access to certain confidential documents on a political level, deputies and senior civil servants, are not permitted to take part in political activities; but the great mass of

Interim Supply
civil servants, including technical and professional personnel, have the right to take part in political activities and many of them do so.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, we want to emphasize our interest in and recognition of the causes of this discontent which finds expression, I understand, in three or four so-called separatist movements in Quebec. While no established political party has adopted the idea of separation of Quebec from Canada, its revival no doubt has certain deep rooted causes which we should understand and recognize.
As I understand it, a number of our French Canadian patriots, Canadians of French descent, consider that their place in confederation has been that of a junior partner. Personally we think they are incorrect in that assumption, but they have that opinion and this lack of understanding is the cause of some discontent. We must appreciate the circumstances which promote these ideas and also, shall I say, to some extent these fears, and we must do all we can to strengthen unity and fraternity on the basis of understanding and a recognition of the principle of equality in all aspects of government and administration.
I am one who believes that we should not get upset about these activities. I must remind the committee that Scotland and Wales have had separatist movements for centuries. In Great Britain they actually provide the places for them to expound their views and talk to their audiences, and they get listened to attentively. They are respected as citizens of Great Britain; not that great numbers agree with them, but they have their rights and they are recognized. Actually, I think just prior to the last coronation some of them stole the coronation stone.
Well, no one in any separatist movement in Canada has suggested stealing anything of a similar kind in Canada, but here is another interesting thing. In Great Britain we find civil and public servants participating in these separatist movements which are the expression of long-standing minor grievances as a result of the union of England with Scotland or England with Wales, and it suggests there is no necessity for people to get concerned and become intolerant because some persons express these views. In Great Britain this is a long-standing tradition.
What about Dr. Chaput about whom there has been this unfortunate publicity? He has not violated his oath of allegiance or of secrecy; he has not violated his oath of office. As a matter of fact, shall I say, on strictly legal grounds the movement is to date nonpartisan because there is no political party in Canada that represents it. Dr. Chaput has

not transgressed any of his constitutional and legal rights as a Canadian citizen or as a public servant.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I did want to bring to the attention of the committee that this group regrets the public statements of the vice-chairman of the defence research board with respect to Dr. Chaput's political activities or whatever you may wish to call them, and the consequent unfortunate publicity. We uphold and defend his right to practice all his privileges as a Canadian citizen and as a public servant, and we urge that the Minister of National Defence announce his support for the practice of the principles of the bill of human freedoms and fundamental rights with respect to all the civil and public servants who come within the jurisdiction of his department.
I am being as brief as possible because we do not wish to lengthen the debate on interim supply. Finally I wish to say with emphasis: Let not the frosts of intolerance wither the blossom of democracy in this country by unfortunate statements or unfortunate publicity.

Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding what the hon. member who has just spoken has had to say I hope he will regard my intervention at this time as wholly within the procedures that we have laid down and within the rights of a member of parliament in accordance with what he thinks are the merits of the situation.
Absolutely.

The hon. member has been speaking on behalf of the freedom of the individual, and that, of course, is a very important matter to engage anyone's consideration. Without in any way commenting on what the hon. member has said I want to say that we in the Liberal party have been discussing this morning a matter that involves not only the freedom of the subject but the freedom of parliament, the rights of parliament and the rights of the people to have from the Minister of Finance an accounting of the financial affairs of the nation.
We offer no apology whatsoever to anyone in the house for persisting in our denunciation of the refusal of the Minister of Finance to give us satisfactory responses. We join heartily once again in support of the position taken by the hon. member for Vancouver East, who in a succinct and able presentation this morning indicated that apparently he appreciates the seriousness of the reluctance of the Minister of Finance to give any indication of when we may expect

the next budget, when we may expect him to give an accounting of the state of the finances of this country.
Though I was not able to put my hands on the specific remarks this morning, I said I had gathered an impression which led me to believe that the Minister of Finance had clearly indicated that he was ready many weeks ago to present his budget. When I pointed that out this morning the hon. member for Greenwood took issue with me and said he did not agree that I could have justifiably formed that impression. He was out of the house when I later produced a question that had been asked by the hon. member for Wellington South and replied to by the Minister of Finance having to do with eliciting from the minister the probable date of the presentation of the budget.
The Minister of Finance replied that he expected to finish hearing delegations by April 8, 1961. We pointed out that in the experience of other governments, certainly no less efficient than this government, once that chore had been completed it had not taken a very great length of time for the minister to come forward and present his budget to the nation. There can be no doubt that if the Minister of Finance had finished hearing delegations by April 8 he was not very far away from the date when he could reasonably be expected to present a budget in this house. I find that later in the session the Minister of Finance gave a further indication that he had reached the point where he was about to present his budget. I find on page 6140 of Hansard for May 1 a question-

We can make a mistake, particularly when it comes to a page of Hansard. The contribution of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance to this debate thus far has consisted of grunts.

He is very close to the Minister of Finance, and if his minister cannot give satisfactory answers I suggest that possibly he might like to take part in the debate and give some indication along the lines which we feel we are entitled to receive and which, as responsibly as we can, we are going to elicit from the government. As found

on page 4140 of Hansard, no less estimable a member than the hon. member for Winnipeg South put this question to the Minister of Finance with regard to the probable date of presentation of the budget:
Mr. Speaker, today being May 1, may I ask the Minister of Finance whether he has as yet fixed the day for the presentation of his budget?
The Minister of Finance said:
No. Mr. Speaker, and I do not think it will be possible to present the budget during the first half of this month.
That question, as was the former question, was put by a member sitting behind those on the ministerial benches. I am not suggesting in this case that it was a planted question because the hon. member for Winnipeg South is quite resourceful and is capable of thinking of questions without even the promptings of the Minister of Finance. The fact is that the former is a member supporting the government. The minister said that he would not be ready during the first half of the month, which leaves open only one conclusion, of course; that he would be ready during the last half of the month of May. This is the 5th of June, and still we have not had from the minister any definite statement when we may expect the budget.
We on this side contend, and we do so with force, that this is an affront to parliament, that this is an affront to the nation as a whole, that business conditions are such as to warrant some assurance from the Minister of Finance that the budget will not be delayed much longer. There is certainly no violation of our traditions in pressing the Minister of Finance to give us some indication when the budget may be presented. We have the right to ask whether there is going to be a budget at all. We have the right to ask within what dates it may be expected, just as did the hon. member for Winnipeg South. The Minister of Finance, in refusing to give us any answer, has left only one real conjecture, the possibility that there will be no budget at all.
If that is the situation, let the government courageously say that in its judgment there is no occasion for a presentation of the financial situation to the nation this year. Let the Minister of Finance say that he is content with the budget brought in on May 18, 1960. There would, of course, be controversy over that position, but at any rate the government would at least have taken some definite position. The Minister of Finance this morning spoke loosely of the relation of the so-called baby budget to the budget which he said may be brought in some time in the course of the next few months.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not say that at all.
