The Minister of Finance says he did not say that at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The record will speak for itself.

My memory of the inaccurate words of the minister is as good as his. My memory is that the minister said this morning that the budget of last December could not be regarded as not related to the budget which may or may not be presented in 1961. Here is what the minister actually said about the relationship of this so-called baby budget. He did not relate it to a future budget at all. It had no relation, he said, to the future. As found at page 1006 of Hansard of December 20, 1960 the minister said this:
As I said earlier in my speech, this is not a full scale budget. It is a series of specific proposals supplementary to the regular budget I brought down last March. It is an integral part of the broad economic policy set forth in the speech from the throne.
That is not what the hon. gentleman said when he interrupted the hon. member for Welland and said that the baby budget was related to a budget that may or may not be brought down some time in 1961. The minister cannot have it both ways. If the statement made by the minister on December 20 and to which I have just referred is the one that is to be accepted, then the minister is bound to bring down a budget this year because, on his own words, the baby budget of 1960 was related to the previous budget of March, 1960. Hence, unless we can get from the minister some definite assurance we run the chance now that we may not only not have a budget before the end of June, or before adjournment, or before the prorogation of parliament, but that in fact we may not have a budget at all during this year 1961. We are entitled to know what the position of the government is in that regard so the business community can be forewarned and so that parliament can take its decisions and formulate its judgment with regard to the policies of the government in that regard.
The situation must be faced. The minister has left us in an unsatisfactory state as a result of the indefinite replies he gave this morning to the hon. member for Laurier and to other hon. members with regard to the date of the budget. I cannot understand why the minister cannot say positively that there will be a budget before the end of June, or before the adjournment of parliament, or before the prorogation of parliament or before this session comes to an end. Why the minister does not rise in his place and give that definite assurance is something I do not understand. If he does not want to tell us that there will be a budget some time

after June 10, why can he not at least rise in his place and say that there will be a budget along about the dates and times that I have specified? I therefore ask the minister the following questions, and I say that his refusal to answer these questions will be regarded by parliament, and properly so, as an affront to parliament.
You are speaking only for yourself.

His refusal to answer these questions will be regarded as an affront to the nation. His refusal to answer these questions will be a discouragement to the business community and to those in avocations concerned with the economic wellbeing of this nation. The questions are as follows. Will a budget be brought down before the end of June, 1961, or before the adjournment of parliament in 1961? The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance is taking these questions down and I will go slowly so that he may have a record.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is quite unnecessary for the hon. gentleman to go slowly.

In that event I will repeat the question. Of course I could consider that remark as a definite indication of the arrogance of this government, but I will leave that remark stand. The minister did not make it and I do not suppose I have the right to attribute to the minister the indiscretions of his parliamentary secretary. Nevertheless I will leave that remark stand, but I will repeat my questions.
(1)	Will a budget be brought down before the end of June, 1961, or before the adjournment of parliament in 1961?
(2)	In that event, will there be an opportunity for a full debate in accordance with our rules before adjournment or prorogation in 1961?
(3)	Will a budget be brought down in 1961 before adjournment or prorogation of parliament?

There are most serious problems and in spite of all the legislation and policies that have been announced and brought into the house by the government during this session, a great deal of which I and other members of this group have supported, we still face very serious problems which have not been met through the medium of the declarations in the speech from the throne or legislation already introduced or policies already announced.
I can assure the Minister of Finance that in my own province of British Columbia there are serious problems. In the month of June there are thousands upon thousands who are still drawing unemployment insurance payments because they cannot find employment and the weekly payment of $36 for a married person is not enough to maintain a halfdecent standard of living. I can assure the minister that in my own city of Vancouver and in my own constituency of Vancouver East family after family has lost or is losing the amenities of life which are almost taken for granted in Canada but which they are losing because they cannot maintain their payments. Those who have tried to establish home ownership have lost or are losing their homes because they cannot keep up the payments and feed their families at the same time.
I say that right now in the month of June not only is that the position of those who are still drawing unemployment insurance benefits but there are thousands who are no longer eligible for such payments and whose positions are desperate. Something has to be done. The speech from the throne is out of the way. The government must be cognizant of the situation so the only place we can look for further consideration of these matters by the government is to a policy statement and that means the budget of the Minister of Finance. The budget not only deals with the situation I have mentioned and the trade situation to which I referred this morning but 
also with such matters as the Columbia river development which has been mentioned briefly. We should know whether there is going to be an answer to that problem this session. We should know whether or not negotiations will reach the position where the treaty can be ratified at this session of the house. If it is not ratified, this will mean a year's delay in engineering, a year's delay at least in the start of construction.
I am not a prophet of gloom or doom. I disagree with the politics of the government but I hope all of us have only one thing in mind, the happiness and security of the people of our country and the taking of immediate action of some kind to meet problems which have arisen in the past and are still with us. So far as policy is concerned, the only answer we can get is from the Minister of Finance through the medium of the budget. I want to emphasize that our representations at this time are not much ado about nothing. I will go so far as to say that the reason we plead for a policy statement through the medium of the budget is that only through such a statement can we find out whether something is going to be done and whether some new policy is going to be introduced.
Perhaps I am a little emotional, Mr. Chairman, but I have just returned from the province of British Columbia. I have met people there and have seen the suffering that still exists. I say that what we are discussing at this time is not much ado about nothing. It is something that concerns the happiness, security and standard of living of the people of our country whether they are unemployed or whether they are old age pensioners. We ask for only one thing, not a statement such as was made a few minutes ago but the acceptance of responsibility by the government in the way that we hope that all members accept and assume their responsibilities so that we can do our job as the elected representatives of those who sent us here.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Would the minister say who is going to determine whether the accused should be charged with capital murder or non-capital murder.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
This is, of course, a very important question. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is right in saying that obviously those who are charged with the administration of justice should have that responsibility. But in discharging that responsibility they are going to have to be able to satisfactorily define the words "planned and deliberate". As there is not going to be any real jurisprudence in this matter for some time, that is, settled jurisprudence, how can we leave it to law officers of the crown in this way?
I am sure all hon. members were impressed the other evening with what the hon. member for Essex West had to say when he expressed his concern about the apposite character of the words "planned and deliberate". Is the problem not going to arise in the minds of many law officers of the crown, in the right of the province?
The minister had no difficulty in answering the question of the hon. member for Essex West. I have looked back on what the hon. member for Essex West had to say and I bear in mind that he has had very considerable experience as a lawyer. If he was concerned, and if there was this difference of opinion which is going to prevail right at the outset, does the minister feel that this matter can be left in this state in the face of this misunderstanding?
I do not know what effect a renewal of the plea made by us for consideration in a committee of this house will have on the minister after the interval of four days of cessation of debate, but I can say to him that since we have debated this matter I have reviewed it with some persons in this country who have had very considerable experience in the prosecution of criminals. Their concern is as great as that of the hon. member for Essex West with regard to the meaning of the words relating to what is a capital murder and what is non-capital murder.
To leave this in the hands of law officers of the crown at this stage, when there is no jurisprudence and when there is no precise definition of the words is, I say, leaving a matter of this sort in the greatest state of uncertainty. This is altogether different than the kind of action that revolves around the cabinet in the exercise of the royal prerogative. There the obligation, while no less important than that contained in deciding the form of prosecution indictment, is entirely different. There is not the same precision required in the mind of a cabinet member as there is determining what is "planned and

Criminal Code
deliberate" in the mind of a person who is to authorize the laying of a charge from which will flow, if found guilty, a punishment involving death or life imprisonment.
I believe that one at least is justified in expressing one's concern again, particularly in view of the fact that we have had some opportunity since this matter was last discussed of reviewing the matter with other interested persons.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the effective answer is that the law officers of the crown in the provinces now have the responsibility, and it is very heavy and serious responsibility, of deciding whether or not a charge of murder or manslaughter will be laid. The same duty, no different in principle will, admittedly, face those responsible, that is, the duty of deciding whether the evidence in the possession of the prosecution will support a charge of capital murder on the one hand or non-capital murder on the other. It may be it will not support a charge of murder at all, or that a charge of manslaughter will be laid. So there is no difference in principle and I doubt whether there is very much difference in degree, because at the present time a decision has to be reached whether to lay a charge of murder or manslaughter, one carrying the penalty of death and the other not. We are now simply subdividing murder into two categories one punishable by death and the other not, so the duty which falls on officers of the crown is in my view no different from that which they have now.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
I agree there is no difference in principle, inasmuch as the crown now has the responsibility of deciding whether to prefer a charge of manslaughter or a charge of murder, but in making that decision the crown now has the assistance of a considerable body of jurisprudence as to what constitutes manslaughter and what constitutes murder. That is clear. What the crown has now to do, which is new and which provokes this question, is to decide in the absence of practice or with the benefit of very meager practice, except, perhaps for the persuasive influence of precedents in the United States, what constitutes planned and deliberate murder. We have had already in our debates a clear expression of differences of opinion with regard to what "planned and deliberate" really means. I took the opinion of one hon. member of this house who, to my knowledge, has had considerable experience in the interpretation of statutes-the hon. member for Essex West-* and in this connection I would remind the minister of a discussion which took place the

other night on this particular matter, a discussion which revealed differences of interpretation. Such differences are going to prevail, I say, in the offices of attorneys general, in the offices of crown prosecutors, when they come to determine what constitutes "planned and deliberate" in the course of deciding, in certain cases of homicide, whether the charge should be in respect of capital or non-capital murder.
The minister may say: I have expressed my views and made myself very clear as to what I mean. It is true that the crown if it wishes to ascertain what is meant by capital murder and non-capital murder may look at the debates of this house for the purpose of elucidating the meaning. They may rely- I am not saying improperly-upon the words of the Minister of Justice. But I would remind the minister that the courts cannot look on our debates here and on the words of the minister in order to determine what "planned and deliberate" means. The courts are themselves going to define the words "planned and deliberate" just as over the years they have given clarification and meaning to the phrase mens rea. To place this initial responsibility in the hands of the law officers at this stage gives reason for concern about the interpretations which will be placed on them in one jurisdiction as opposed to another-I am not saying this will necessarily happen.
I had a very important criminal lawyer in the province of Ontario tell me the other day that in a discussion of these words with a number of lawyers including an official connected with the office of a law enforcement agency there were three different opinions expressed as to what was meant by the words "planned and deliberate". The minister is not resolving this problem simply by saying he is leaving it to the officials charged with the administration of justice. That has not settled the matter. It can only be settled humanly by making sure that we have resorted to phraseology which is capable of the strictest meaning in accordance with the capacity of the human mind to formulate words which represent as accurately as possible the purpose that one has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
May I just answer the observations of the hon. gentleman before the hon. member for Vancouver South speaks? I am not saying that this is the final answer to the problem but we have, of course, endeavoured, and, I believe, with success to use words which are in themselves a precise definition of the kind of murder which will be capital murder from now on. It is true that jurisprudence will be built up with regard to this new category of murder as, of course, jurisprudence is built up as a result of any substantial amendment to the criminal

law. This does not mean that we should not go ahead and make this new subdivision of murders into categories, making clear at the same time what it is that constitutes the difference between the two categories as we have done here. I would point out, for instance, that in the United States when murder was first divided into degrees this was a new concept. In the commonwealth of Pennsylvania whose provision in this respect has been the basic one upon which all the others, generally speaking, have been founded, it was laid down that-
-all murder, which shall be perpetrated by means of poison, or by lying in wait, or by any other kinds of wilful, deliberate and premeditated killing, or which shall be committed in the perpetration or attempt to perpetrate-
Then follow a number of offences.
-shall be deemed murder of the first degree.
In my submission, the words "wilful, deliberate and premeditated" were no easier to interpret than are the words "planned or deliberate". But the legislature in Pennsylvania did not shrink from saying them and making a departure from the previous law when they thought it was appropriate to do so, having taken the precaution of indicating, as definitely as their legislature then could, precisely what it had in mind and what must be proven in order to constitute the subdivision of murder.
I said a moment ago that the crown officers will have a duty no different from that which now falls upon them. The duty they have now is to decide whether to lay a charge of murder or one of manslaughter. In future they will have to decide whether the charge shall be capital murder, noncapital murder or manslaughter. Cases may arise in the future, just as they do now, where there will be difficulty in reaching a decision. In that case the authorities can lay a charge of capital murder on the basis of which the jury may convict of capital murder, or non-capital murder if they feel that the graver charge is not proven, just as now a charge of murder may be laid and the jury may convict of manslaughter if they feel the charge of murder has not been proven. I do not deny that there may be cases where this will be the only proper course for the crown to follow. In general, however, it is our view that the accused should be charged with the offence for which he is to be tried. That is why we have provided that if a man is to be convicted of capital murder he must be charged with capital murder.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Justice has, at least in part, covered what I have to say. I find myself in a position similar to that of the hon. member for Essex East,
Criminal Code
in that I am slightly worried about the actual wording of clause 3, which reads as follows:
No person shall be convicted of capital murder unless in the indictment charging the offence he is specifically charged with capital murder.
That gives me a little concern. I am not a member of the legal profession and naturally have taken the opportunity, since this bill was introduced, of consulting with members of the legal profession who are experienced in the law, and particularly in cases involving homicide. I find myself having to accept the advice they have given me, and should say at the outset that I think it is sensible.
Those individuals have pointed out to me that the person responsible for drafting an indictment, even as the law now exists, must have a decision whether the charge should involve a conviction and sentence for capital murder, or manslaughter, which carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. Those advisers also pointed out to me another matter which I think is of concern. I hope the hon. member for Essex East will follow this situation. It has been suggested that with the adoption of this new law there will be no backlog of jurisprudence and, therefore, it should not be adopted. I suggest if that were the case, we could never make any advance in legislation. This represents a new law and will have to be interpreted. I therefore suggest the argument falls completely to the ground.
One other point, which was brought to my attention by those members of the legal profession with whom I spoke, has been partially covered by the Minister of Justice this afternoon. When an officer of the crown decides to draft an indictment which involves capital punishment and the evidence shows that it was incorrectly drafted, I am advised that it is then within the power of the judge to give direction to the jury, making certain recommendations and, under the proposed act, the jury will have the authority to bring in the finding that murder, in a capital sense, is not involved but rather homicide in the other sense, or manslaughter. In fairness I think I should state that, having consulted several members of the legal profession, I have been advised by them unanimously that the situation I have just outlined is the fact, and I, therefore, have to accept the wording as contained in this bill.
On clause 4-Pleas permitted.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in respect of clause 4 I should like to say that I have some concern. Not being a member of the legal fraternity-thank	God, perhaps-I
should like the minister to explain the portion of this clause which reads as follows:

Criminal Code
An accused who is charged with an offence punishable by death and is called upon to plea may plead not guilty, or the special pleas authorized by this part and no others.
It was my understanding that when a charge was laid against an individual in court there were only two pleas which could be taken, guilty or not guilty. I should like to ask the minister to explain the use of the words "may plead not guilty or the special pleas".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the pleas are autrefois acquit, autrefois convict, or pardon.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Could you put that in English?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: That is to say, that the accused has already been tried for the same offence and acquitted-that is autrefois acquit; that he has already been tried for the same offence and convicted, that is autrefois convict; or that he has been pardoned for the offence. Those are the three special pleas. If either one of them is established, the case is disposed of and there is no trial.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Thank you very much.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not understand the wording of (2a) which reads as follows:
An accused who Is charged with an offence punishable by death and is called upon to plea may plead not guilty,-
The word "may" seems to be in contradiction of other sections of the act because it is a right that an accused can plead not guilty. Why is the word "may" or, in French, "pent" used there?

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the same
thought occurred to me because that portion is tied in with clause 5 which also states that the accused may plead not guilty, although in that case it is when he is charged with an offence other than one which is punishable by death.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, an accused must plead something. The law provides that he may plead-the word "only" is not in the code but I use it here-he may plead only not guilty or the special pleas authorized by this act, and that is all he can do. Those are the only pleas he can give which will be accepted.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Why do you not use the word "shall" then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: This clause has been written to conform with the present wording of the section which we are actually amending. The effect of it is that on a charge of capital murder an accused cannot plead guilty.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not raise this argument now, but it will be said by some that a jury will know that an accused could not plead guilty and will be influenced, therefore, to some extent in its decision. I do not raise that argument as my own, but possibly to elicit some comment from the minister which will assure other hon. members of this committee. The point is that because an accused cannot plead guilty a jury might be influenced.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not able to follow that argument or appreciate it because the statute provides that certain pleas only can be entered, and I do not see how the jury could be prejudiced or influenced by that fact. The statute should provide only what the pleas are that may be entered, and in this instance it does provide what they may be. This is quite different, and it is an important difference or distinction, from saying by statute that the accused shall enter a plea of so and so. That distinction to our minds is important. Therefore, we have said that in the case of an accused charged with capital murder he may enter one of three special pleas, or a plea of not guilty.

If my hon. friend will permit me to complete the sentence. He will find, if he reads clause 4, that a plea of guilty may not be accepted; that is, a plea of guilty to a charge of capital murder. If he does not plead not guilty, or one of the special pleas authorized by this part or does not answer directly, the court shall order the clerk of the court to enter a plea of not guilty. I do not think anything could be much clearer than that.
First of all he is given his option to enter any one of four pleas, not guilty, or one of the three special pleas. If he does not enter one of those pleas, or if he stays silent, then the court orders that the plea to be entered shall be not guilty. That is perfectly clear and to my mind a readily understandable method of providing in the proper legal phraseology that there cannot be a plea of guilty to a charge of capital murder accepted by the court.

speechtext:
I should like to make some remarks with respect to this clause and ask the minister some questions. The effect of this clause, of course, is to make non-capital murder an included offence in a capital murder charge. May I suggest to the minister that the necessary practical effect of this is going to be that every crown counsel throughout the country will not decide beforehand whether he is going to get a conviction for capital murder or otherwise. What he will do in every instance is to charge capital murder because this will probably prevent the escape of any accused person. It has been my experience both in my reading and in my practice that the crown counsel never charges manslaughter under present circumstances. He always charges murder and uses this as a basis of a possible reduced plea. Since the effect of all these sections together is that it is not possible to accept a plea of guilty in capital murder, the pressure will be on the defence counsel and on the accused, if, as will happen in every case, the crown counsel lays a charge of capital murder, to remove any

Criminal Code
possibility of a death sentence, and therefore there will be a guilty plea on a reduced charge of non-capital murder.
I would suggest to the minister that this might well be considered before the discussion on the bill is concluded, and that if noncapital murder were not an included offence, but if the option was taken away so that there could only be a conviction, if there had been separate counts charged in the indictment. In other words, that non-capital murder be not an included offence, but that there must be a specific charge in the indictment, one for capital murder and one for non-capital murder. This will prevent the possibility of dickers being made to get a guilty plea on the lesser charge.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take issue with the statement made by the hon. member for Niagara Falls. It has been my experience in at least three cases that I can lay my mind to that in the cases which were charged with murder, the original preliminary inquiries were held where all the facts were ventilated. When it appeared on the examination of those facts that the graver charge was not justified the attorney general's department reduced the charges so far as the indictment was concerned, and when the accused appeared before the jury he appeared on a charge of manslaughter and was tried on that charge.
It has been my experience that most agents of attorneys general, or crown counsel are responsible people who are determined to see that the charge which is laid is one which meets the facts. However, I should like to ask the minister this question. Am I correct in assuming that clause 7 as amending section 569 will leave five alternatives? If a charge is laid in respect of capital murder, will there be these five various alternatives open, capital murder, non-capital murder, manslaughter, not guilty by reason of insanity and not guilty? Would all of these five alternatives then be available if a charge is laid for capital murder pursuant to this amending clause?

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
May I just follow up where the hon. gentleman left off. I recognize that in doing so we are not giving the minister the opportunity to deal with the point raised by the hon. member for Niagara Falls, with which I hope he will deal. As I understand clause 7, it would appear from the proposed amendment that on a charge of capital murder there are seven findings open to a jury: guilty of capital murder, guilty of attempted capital murder, guilty of non-capital murder, guilty of attempted non-capital murder, guilty of manslaughter, guilty of infanticide or not guilty. I have had some

difficulty with this clause. Is this as far as that clause goes? If this is the correct interpretation, has the minister given consideration that the jury might make a finding of manslaughter if the facts warranted it?

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Could I ask how a person can be guilty of attempted capital murder? I do not quite understand that. If you have committed murder, how can you be guilty of attempted capital murder?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: The conviction, as I see it, would be related to an attempt to commit capital murder. That is a perfectly well understood principle.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: And if you are found guilty the penalty is death?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
You are only liable to the death penalty if you have killed someone and it is found to be capital murder, but the code does provide that a person may also be charged with an attempt to commit that offence and may be found guilty of an attempt to commit that offence. That is the situation in respect of a verdict of guilty of an attempt to commit the crime.
On the question of whether or not there should be two counts included in the same indictment, which was the point raised by the hon. member for Niagara Falls, it seems to me there would be certain objections. In the first place, the two charges are mutually exclusive. The person was either guilty of capital murder or of non-capital murder. He could not be guilty of both. Therefore it seems to me we would have to charge them in their alternatives and you would have one trial. We think that is undesirable, however, particularly in a case of this seriousness where it seems to me to be only appropriate that the crown should itself determine what is the charge for which the accused is going to be placed on trial. If he is going to be on trial for his life, the crown should so charge it. Alternatively, if he is only going to be placed on trial for an offence that involves life imprisonment he should know that and he should actually be placed on trial as the result of a charge accordingly. He should not have to meet them both either concurrently, which I think would be impossible, or alternatively. We think the crown should make up its mind and lay the charge accordingly.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
May I say that I quite agree with the last words of the minister. If I were satisfied that in all provinces the practice was followed which one of my colleagues informs me is the practice in Alberta I would agree that this is the best sort of thing. The best way would be if crown counsel in the very first instance would make up their minds whether they are going to prosecute for

Criminal Code
capital murder or non-capital. Failing that, perhaps it would be possible to follow the practice that apparently is followed in Alberta whereby a preliminary hearing is held and, on the basis of the evidence adduced at that hearing, crown counsel would decide to reduce the charge if the evidence would only support non-capital murder. This would at least mean that the trial before the jury would be only on the basis of that which the crown was able to prove. While I do not have any statistics with me to this effect, I think it will be found that at least in the province of Ontario the practice is that murder is always charged and is only reduced either as a result of the grand jury procedure or as a result of a plea taken or of directions and the jury's decision.
The hon. member for Vancouver East mentioned another point about an attempt. I am not able to find in the code at the moment exactly what the penalty is for an attempt. Although my recollection is not very clear, I believe that the maximum penalty for an attempt in the case of an indictable offence is half the maximum penalty if the offence has been completed. Perhaps the minister will recall that point. You cannot half kill some one, of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: I must apologize to the hon. member. I was not able to follow what the hon. lady was saying.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Does the minister remember what the general penalty is for an attempt at an offence?

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Section 210, to which I have been referred, reads as follows:
Every one who attempts by any means to commit murder is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life.
I notice no amendment in the bill before us today to provide a difference between capital and non-capital murder in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
We do not think it is necessary. Obviously you would not impose the death penalty for an attempt to commit capital murder because there would be no life taken. Therefore the maximum penalty would be life imprisonment. This section provides that an accused convicted of an attempt to commit murder is liable to life imprisonment. The hon. member for Niagara Falls will remember that the definition of murder is not changed by this bill. What is new in the bill is that murder, if proven, is in turn divided into capital and non-capital. So all you would have to prove in the future, as has been the case in the past, is an attempt to commit murder and then, whatever kind of murder the accused may have intended, he is still liable to life 90205-6-372
imprisonment. We did not think any amendment was necessary under the situation as it exists.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: I wished to draw the minister's attention to the matter because the apparent raison d'etre behind the whole amendment now before the committee is that there seems to be a gradation of guilt between those crimes which are premeditated and those which are not. Thus there should also be a gradation between those attempts at intentional crimes and the other types.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: I do not think so because the gradation here is where a life has been taken. Where a life has been taken and it is found to be murder, murder is then divided into capital and non-capital and the death penalty or life imprisonment follows respectively. But that is dealing with the case where life has been taken, that is, murder has been accomplished. The offence to which the hon. member is now directing her mind is the offence of attempting to commit murder and there the law already provides a penalty of life imprisonment. It seems to me that is the maximum penalty that it would be desirable to provide at any time for a crime which does not succeed or result in the taking of life. For that reason we did not think there was any necessity to amend that section, bearing in mind that whether it is capital murder or non-capital murder it still must be murder. Therefore it is not necessary in the charge of attempt to commit murder to say whether the accused intended capital or non-capital murder. All he has to attempt is murder and then he is liable to a penalty up to life imprisonment.

Assuming the incapacity to prove any one of these six categories of guilt, why should the jury not be specifically authorized to make a finding of manslaughter if the facts warrant it?

Subject to subsection 3, where a count charges murder and the evidence proves manslaughter or infanticide but does not prove murder, the jury may find the accused not guilty of murder-

Criminal Code

2. Subject to subsection (3), where a count charges capital or non-capital murder and the evidence proves manslaughter or infanticide but does not prove murder, the jury may find the accused not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter-

I am a little bit puzzled about clause 8 and the exact meaning of it. I am now referring to subclause 2 which reads as follows:
A person who has been sentenced to death shall-
If I understand the matter correctly, the only persons who may be sentenced to death according to the Criminal Code or according to the bill before us are those guilty of culpable killing for instance, while committing piracy or capital murder. In cases of that kind sentence is imposed by law. The other instance would be in the case of treason. The clause reads as follows:
(2) A person who has been sentenced to death shall, notwithstanding he has not given notice pursuant to section 586, be deemed to have given such notice and to have appealed against his conviction and against his sentence unless that sentence is one fixed by law.
Will the minister tell us exactly what the meaning of that subclause is? Is or is not a man who is found guilty of capital murder able to appeal against the sentence or should he appeal only against the conviction? What about the other instance in which a man is found guilty of treason?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
The answer is that in the case of a conviction for capital murder he would not be able to appeal against his sentence. He would only be able to appeal against the verdict. That is, of course the case of most concern. The situation is similar wherever the sentence is one fixed by law, where it is a mandatory sentence. However, in the case of treason, as provided in section 47 of the code, my hon. friend will note that there the sentence is optional. The section provides:
47. (1) Every one who commits treason is guilty of an Indictable offence and Is liable-
I would direct my hon. friend's attention to subparagraph (b).
- (b) to be sentenced to death or to imprisonment for life if he is guilty of an offence under paragraph (d),	(f) or (g) of subsection (1) of
section 46;
Obviously as to a person who was convicted of treason and sentenced to death, it is only appropriate that such person would have the right to appeal against the sentence as well as the finding.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Will the minister indicate how this is going to work under clause 9? Suppose we have the case of a man who has been sentenced to death but whose execution has been fixed for a certain date. Where is the line of demarcation? He has a right of appeal. Can the minister indicate how this is going to work? Can he give us an example?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
The explanatory note makes clear that the purpose is to ensure that where-ever a sentence of death has been imposed, the execution of the sentence will be suspended until after the termination of the appeal which is now provided as of right and indeed automatically to the court of appeal of the province. I would think that such a provision as that which we have in clause 9 is necessary, because the date of execution still must be fixed, and even although the judge imposing the sentence may have allowed what he regards as, and what under ordinary circumstances would be, ample time for the conclusion of the appeal, there may arise circumstances that would have the result that the appeal is not disposed of by the date fixed for the execution. The clause now before us makes it perfectly clear that if that situation should transpire then the date of execution is automatically postponed and a new date set on application to a judge who might have presided at the trial at which the accused was sentenced.
Another clause also makes it clear, and I think provides for the first time in specific

terms, that the application for extension or postponement of the date of execution does not have to be heard by the judge who actually presided at the trial. There was in Ontario one case which was a very difficult one indeed, where the judge who presided at the trial I think was away on holidays or ill and a very real question arose as to whether another judge of the trial division had the right to postpone the date of execution. We do not wish that sort of difficulty or uncertainty to arise again. Hence, in addition to providing an automatic right of extension, another clause makes it clear that any judge of the trial division who could have presided at the trial may extend the time.

I think that is a necessary and good provision. However, I am wondering whether the language is not a little bit dangerous. The clause states:
-it may be fixed by the judge who imposed the sentence or any judge who might have held or sat in the same court.
That language could be open to any interpretation. A judge might find himself sitting in weekly court when obviously it is not intended that he should be the judge who should have the right of providing for a stay of execution or of fixing another date. Obviously, what is meant is a judge of the same jurisdiction or a judge of co-ordinate jurisdiction such as judges of the trial division of the supreme court, but not "any judge who might have held or sat in the same court". The judge may be a retired judge or it might be a judge in admiralty sitting in a court of general sessions or something of that sort. This is an ambiguous phrase. I think what we really mean is that the judge who shall have the power to fix another date must be a judge of the same order as the judge who imposed the sentence in the first instance. If that is the case, I think that is what we ought to say.

Where a judge who sentences a person to death considers-

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make some comments on clause 13. Perhaps it may seem rather strange that I, a person totally opposed to capital punishment, should be discussing the legalities which arise in this bill which will have the effect of putting a man to death, but I suppose that is one of the paradoxes of being a member of parliament.
I must admit that clause 13 made me do quite a bit of soul searching because there is a very important principle involved here. May I say in the first instance that on balance I think I agree with the principle and support of clause 13, but I would appreciate hearing from the minister and other hon. members their views about this.
Under this section we have this provision: Where a jury finds an accused guilty of an offence punishable by death, the judge who presides at the trial shall, before discharging the jury, put to them the following question:
You have found the accused guilty and the law requires that I now pronounce sentence of death against him-*
Then the judge adds:	,
Do you wish to make any recommendation as to whether or not he should be granted clemency.
As I see it, we are placing a dual responsibility on the jury. First of all the jury has to decide whether or not the person before the bar is guilty of homicide of a nature which carries the death penalty. That is a mighty grave responsibility to place upon a jury, and only the jury can decide that matter. They know they are actually, within the strict terms of the law, deciding

whether a man or woman shall live or die. I, personally, should hate to be placed in that position, but society demands that this course be followed and I think it is correct that it should. Having found a person guilty, the question is put to them whether they make, or do not make, any recommendation for clemency. On first reading this clause it was my impression that if a recommendation for clemency was forthcoming from the jury the governor general in council would have recourse to the royal prerogative and commute the sentence to one of life imprisonment.
I regret I was not able to be here when the previous discussion took place on second reading, but I understand through reading the newspapers that this point of view was confirmed by a statement of the Prime Min-nister-that in future all recommendations of clemency made by juries would be accepted by the governor general in council and that the sentence of death would automatically be commuted. We are, therefore, in this situation: under the terms of this clause not only is the jury responsible for deciding whether a person is guilty or innocent but, in addition, it must decide, in effect, whether, having found a person guilty, the penalty is to be carried out. If they say nothing they are, in effect, saying "death", unless, of course, clemency is exercised by the governor general in council in exceptional circumstances. If the jury recommends clemency they are saying that the sentence shall be one of life imprisonment. Perhaps this is as it should be. On balance I have had to come to the decision that this is the correct principle to follow, but I want to add that a great deal of soul searching was necessary before I could bring myself to agree that this double responsibility should be placed on juries as distinct from the responsibility placed upon them in the past when they had only to decide whether a person was guilty or innocent, it being then the responsibility of the governor general in council, reviewing all the evidence and all the circumstances, to decide whether or not clemency should be invoked.
From the wording of the clause as it stands it appears that the government is accepting what I understand to be the principle in Californian law where the same procedure must be followed. I am afraid I am getting repetitious, but I have been distinctly worried about this clause and I should like to hear the minister explain the basic reasoning which led him to draft this clause in its present form. As I say, I think it should be supported. On the other hand I should like to hear a little more about the reasoning behing the placing of this double responsibility on juries.

I am convinced that the meaning of this clause is not clear and that its interpretation would give the courts a great deal of difficulty. It has always been our law that a jury when acquitting or convicting a person charged with a crime must reach a unanimous decision. If they do not, a disagreement is recorded. In the past, juries have on occasion brought in recommendations of mercy on their own initiative. Our juries, I believe, attempt to agree to a much greater extent than do juries in the United States, and perhaps this is a good thing. In any event, most lawyers who have had a great deal of experience in the practice of criminal law-I cannot profess to be in that category-tell me that often recommendations for mercy in this country represent a compromise. It may be that a few jurymen hold out for a conviction while a few are in favour of acquittal; agreement is then reached that a finding of guilty shall be returned with a recommendation of mercy.
The clause as now drawn is a complete departure, as I understand it, from the present conception of the roles of the judge and the jury. It was for the jury alone to determine the guilt or innocence of the accused; they have had no part in the sentencing of the accused, and the judge, being presumed to be one of great experience, was the person to whom had been delegated the responsibility of determining the sentence. Now we are changing that. Under clause 13, a question is to be put to the jury regarding any recommendation for clemency. I ask the minister -and a reply to this question is, it seems to me, important-is a unanimous vote required, as in a determination of guilt or innocence? Suppose one juror is against clemency being granted while 11 are in favour? Would there be an announcement of a disagreement of this kind. The wording is not clear. I think consideration should be given to asking the jury to record a majority vote on this question. The jury should therefore be asked whether a majority of their number is in favour of making a recommendation for clemency. Otherwise, I am told, there will be a great deal of confusion on this point, certainly with good reason, because there is no authority here for a judge to take the initiative himself in determining whether a majority or unanimity is required.
It seems to me that the clause can be clarified by an amendment, if it is thought desirable to leave it in its present form. I shall be prepared to speak to it later but I put it forward now for the purpose of discussion, at least.

The amendment does not take into account he question which I myself raised concerning unanimity or a majority of opinion on the part of the jury in favour of clemency. Mr. Chairman, one of the provisions of this proposed act which is alarming to me is contained in clause 13 of the bill before us. The minister is undoubtedly aware of the procedure which takes place in a court room, but I hope he will forgive me if I outline a part of it for the benefit of those members of this committee who are not familiar with that procedure.
For instance, hon, members may not be aware that a murder jury, whether the case involves capital murder or non-capital murder, is locked up, whether it be for hours or overnight, until it has reached a verdict and presented it to the court. When it has reached a verdict the jury is brought back into the open court room in the presence of the accused's counsel, members of the public and press, at which time, having presented its verdict, the provisions of this clause would be read. Whether the verdict presented represents a majority decision or a unanimous one, defence counsel has the opportunity of polling the members of the jury as to its verdict. The judge will then ask the members of the jury whether or not they wish to recommend clemency. I suggest that is a departure from the principles of justice because there should not be any suggestion made to a jury that they recommend against clemency.

I suggest most juries in Canada are sufficiently sophisticated to know that there exist instances when clemency can be recommended.
In many cases, although during the charge from the justice to the jury nothing was said regarding their right to make recommendations, the jury has come back into the court room, following deliberation and before announcing their verdict, asking if they had a right to do so. Juries are then informed that they of course can do so. They then are returned to the jury room where they decide this question.
Under the situation which will exist by the adoption of clause 13 of this bill before us, the question as to whether a jury recommends clemency or not, will be asked by the justice following delivery of their verdict. In other words the jurymen would be sitting in open court when the question was asked. I ask hon. members of this committee to consider what might then well happen. No deliberation in those circumstances could have been made in regard to such a recommendation nor would there be the opportunity afforded members of the jury to discuss this matter among themselves. The question having been asked of the jury, the foreman might well be startled, turn to the jurymen behind him, and then give an answer to the question which may or may not represent the opinion of the rest of the members of the jury. He may recommend clemency, or may recommend against it. In any event, whichever he does, it may not be the unanimous feeling of those gentlemen sitting behind him. That being the case, another member of that jury could stand up and inform the court that it was not representative of his opinion. It must be remembered that this would take place in open court without the jury having been afforded an opportunity to deliberate on this most crucial point.
I suggest the situation which I have alluded to is important particularly in view of the Prime Minister's statement a day or two ago that a recommendation for clemency would be tantamount to an escape from the gallows. I should hope that what the Prime Minister said could not be interpreted as being indicative that a recommendation against clemency would be tantamount to closing the door ensuring that the individual would hang.
Nevertheless, and because of the great importance being attached, not only by the Minister of Justice, but by the Prime Minister as expressed in his speech, to this particular feature of the new legislation, I suggest that a law, which could be taken as standing between an accused and the gallows, should not be interpreted by a judge so that such a question could be put to a jury in a casual

way, in an open court room, the jury not having the opportunity to deliberate and discuss the matter.
Hr. Chairman, in the consideration of a subject as vital as this, disregarding the question as to whether or not the cabinet is shirking its responsibility by placing this decision upon the shoulders of individuals in local communities who make up juries, the phraseology used in this clause should be designed in such a way as to require the judge to inform the jury, without undue emphasis one way or the other, that it has the right Jo recommend or not recommend clemency, during that portion of the trial when the judge is charging the jury as to the law. If such were the case, when a jury had deliberated and decided whether the facts established a capital charge, it could then deliberate and discuss the question of recommending clemency, which would then be reported to the court, following the announcement of the jury's verdict.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this amendment because I feel it should not be supported and I will vote against it. The basic trouble with the proposed amendment is that it will confuse the jury. Under the jury system, the first duty of the jury, or of the judge when he is sitting alone, is to find whether or not the accused is guilty of the crime with which he is charged. The question of sentence or of punishment should not come into it whatsoever while the jury, or the judge when sitting alone, is deciding the innocence or guilt of the party charged. As the act stands now, this is exactly what happens. The jury first decide the guilt or innocence of the accused and report their finding to the judge. At that point they are not confused in any way with the question of punishment or with the result of their finding.
It is very easy for a judge-or it should be easy for him-to keep the two problems before him separate in his mind, but it is not easy for a jury. They have a great many problems to consider when they are trying to determine whether or not an accused is guilty. I think it is fairly simple after they have brought in their finding of guilty of capital murder. They have carried out this part of their duty and the only part that they have normally to decide by law. However, after having sat on a jury trial for perhaps several days, or a week, they have heard all the evidence that has been given and they have come to a conclusion as to guilt. They are also qualified at that particular moment to come to some decision on the question of clemency. But the time at which they must direct their minds to it is after they have made their decision on the guilt of the accused. Therefore, having delivered their finding, they are asked a second question.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls pointed up the difficulty that might arise but I cannot agree with her that it is likely to arise. There is no reason on earth why the jury, having been asked the second question, if they wish to make a recommendation of clemency, ought not then to retire again to

the jurors' room and consider this second question. I can understand that they should not decide right away while they are sitting in their seats the way they do when they are selecting a foreman, which I think is what the hon. member had in mind. We often find that a jury will look around and see some person there whom they all know, and somebody says "We appoint a certain person foreman", which is really not a matter about which they even need to leave the courtroom. But when it comes to the matter of clemency, I could not possibly see how a jury would right offhand make a finding of clemency. They should then again retire.
However, if there is any feeling that the clause is not clear or that some confusion might arise, perhaps it could be clarified to the point where the jury should be asked to retire again to the jury room. Frankly, I do not see that it should be necessary. I think a judge would deal with them in the same way as he does when they come in and ask for further directions. He would merely be giving them further instructions as to their duty. They would again retire to the jury room and take as long as they felt necessary to come to a conclusion.
I think the bill as drafted is perfectly satis-actory. The amendment would do no more than confuse the jurors as between the two duties that they are being asked to perform.

As I said a few moments ago, I found this section very complex. Now that the amendment is before us I find it very ticklish and difficult to come to a decision. Basically, I like the idea of the amendment in that the decision as to guilt and recommendation for clemency would be arrived at at one and the same time; but I can also see a certain complication which I am not certain that I like. For this reason I personally would like to get a greater exposition of the reasons why the amendment should be accepted. I make this request for two reasons. If the amendment carries we shall have the clause as amended. Although this may seem a little far fetched, I still think that by reason of the judge making this statement in his charge to the jury, there will be, whether we like it or not, a little pre-supposition of guilt. I say that because we find the word "if" is included. He is not yet found guilty or innocent but if he is found guilty, then two courses are open. As I said, it may be a little far-fetched but there is an implication there of the supposition of guilt. I wish there were a psychologist here. I say there is psychologically enough here to make an impression on a juror's mind. This is the first faint doubt which comes to my mind with respect to the amendment.
There is a second doubt which to me is a little more important. If the clause is amended

as suggested we will have the jury sitting in camera and at one and the same time considering the guilt or innocence and punishment of the accused. I have done a great deal of reading on matters which pertain to homicide and juries. If my understanding of what I have read is correct, it is quite conceivable that a lot of bargaining will go on during the deliberations of the jury. They will sit there hour after hour trying to reach a decision and one juror will say, "Very well, I will vote for guilty if you will vote for clemency and mercy". I think it is almost certain that will happen so therefore the function of the jury in determining only the guilt or innocence of the accused is being undermined. There will be bargaining or compromise with respect to guilt or innocence, and I do not think that is what is intended by our law. In the light of what I said a few moments ago when we first discussed this question, these two perplexing questions come to my mind. I hope I have laid sufficient groundwork so that those who favour this procedure will rise and expound further on why it should be accepted and whether there are arguments against the two points I have raised and tried to make clear.

Mr. Chairman, the reasons why we made the change in the law in the form of the amendment as we now have it, have been admirably summarized by the hon. member for Vancouver East, and it is for those reasons that I would be unable to agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Essex East in moving his amendment. I also bring to the argument that I want to advance the views expressed by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka.
First, we felt that it was appropriate that the jury should be asked whether they had a recommendation to make. That is the first thing, and I will come back to the reasons why we feel that is appropriate in a moment. I want to deal now with the stage at which the jury should be asked that question. After most careful reflection we feel very strongly that they should not be asked to consider that question while at the same time they are considering the question of the guilt or innocence of the accused. These are two entirely separate things and the first thing that juries should be asked to decide is, is this man guilty of the charge or is he not guilty?
I do not think I can do much better than the two hon. members to whom I have referred have done in attempting to indicate why we feel it is inappropriate that the two questions should be mixed, but perhaps this additional argument is relevant. Surely if the crown prosecutor referred in any way to the
Criminal Code
possibility of commutation or the exercise of the royal prerogative of mercy it would be grounds for a new trial. It would be quite improper for him to try to suggest to the jury, come on, you might as well bring in a verdict of guilty because there is always a review by the cabinet and the possibility of commutation. This, of course, would be objected to and I am quite sure that even though it was ordered to be stricken from the record it would still be grounds for a new trial. It would be a most improper thought to intrude into the minds of the jury at a time when they were asked to consider whether or not the man was guilty as charged or innocent. I will not use the word "improper" in connection with the amendment and I am not suggesting for a moment that it is offered improperly in any sense but I think it would be unwise to adopt it because if carried into effect it would import an improper element to be considered by the jury, that is, improper for their consideration at the time when they are deliberating their verdict because it certainly could not fail to open to their minds the possibility that the matter is not so very serious after all if they find him guilty in that they can make a recommendation of clemency I think this is very dangerous and it would be a bad thing to import into the minds of the jury at that stage.
But I see nothing improper at all or unfair to juries, having brought in their verdict as a result of a process of deliberation in which their minds have been exclusively directed to the question of guilt or innocence, that it should subsequently be said to them, "You have brought in your verdict and have satisfied yourselves and reported accordingly that the accused is guilty; do you or do you not have a recommendation to make with regard to the exercise of clemency"?
It is true that this does then place another duty upon the jury, that of considering whether or not clemency should be shown but, as I have indicated before, this is not a duty which it is improper, unwise or unfair to ask the jury to discharge. As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka said, they have perhaps sat for days and have heard all the evidence. They are the twelve peers who have been asked to decide whether their fellow human being is guilty or innocent of the offence charged. Surely, therefore, they are proper persons to be asked subsequently while the evidence is still fresh in their minds, including the evidence brought forward by the defence, "You have found the accused guilty of the crime of capital murder; notwithstanding that, do you nevertheless feel that there is something in what you have heard that in your judgment would warrant

Criminal Code
a recommendation that the royal prerogative of mercy be exercised and clemency shown"?
With respect to the question of whether or not they should deliberate that problem in open court, I agree with the hon. member for Niagara Falls that it would be very inappropriate for them either to attempt to reach a snap verdict or to find themselves in controversy in open court, but I agree fully with the hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka that it would be quite natural for the judge to suggest to them or invite them to retire to deliberate their decision on this matter just as they deliberated on their verdict. I do not think that poses any problem.
Perhaps the remaining problem is the question of whether or not the jury should be asked to do this and there I direct hon. member's attention to the findings of the Gowers royal commission. I agree that its findings are not the final word with respect to what should be done in Canada especially but nevertheless a group of very experienced judges and jurists came to the conclusion that indeed it was not only not wrong to ask the jury whether or not they thought clemency should be exercised but they also felt it was not wrong to ask the jury to determine what the sentence should be. They suggested that if the jury brought in a verdict of guilty they should then be asked whether the sentence should be death or life imprisonment. We certainly do not go that far. We think that would be wrong in that the law itself should provide the penalty automatically, but we feel it is perfectly proper for the jury to be asked whether they have an opinion or recommendation as to clemency.
I have one further word before six o'clock. Some suggestion has been made that the Prime Minister said that a recommendation for mercy would automatically be followed by commutation. I cannot find that anywhere in his statement made in the house on May 29. I do not know whether it is based on these words which I find at the bottom of page 5527:
Having heard the evidence and having come to the conclusion on the basis of the law as explained to them by the judge that a verdict of guilty is the only one they can bring in, a jury ought none the less to have the right to add a recommendation to mercy, and having done that, to hope that the royal prerogative will be reasonably carried out.

The minister then replies and says there is no provision. I urge that there should be a provision and I inquire of the minister what was the intention of the minister since no reference was made to the possibility of a divided judgment. Suppose the jury had divided, as the hon. member for Welland has indicated, one for and eleven against. In that event will the section become operative? Will effect be given to the decision of the majority? In the case of the determination as to guilt the rule of unanimity applies and, in my opinion, wisely so. But in a matter of secondary importance- secondary in the sense that it is not as important as is the question of guilt-it is reasonable to argue that there will be some misunderstanding.
I can understand the minister being concerned about making a provision for it. The minister may possibly want to leave that matter to chance and to allow a practice to develop. However, I doubt whether that practice can eventuate because unless the jury know positively that a majority will be sufficient, they will not act; and unless the judge knows that a majority will be sufficient, he will not permit it to eventuate. Thus the purpose might be seriously defeated. In other words now is the time for us to meet this ambiguity and the ambiguity is there. Does the rule of unanimity apply? There is in this clause nothing that enables us to give a satisfactory answer to this question.
The point I sought to raise was that we should deal with the matter forthrightly and should indicate whether or not the majority or unanimity rule was required. Personally, in the case of clemency, I would think that where a majority of the jury recommended for clemency, it ought to operate. The minister may not have that view but he can state his position. However, we should not leave this section in the ambiguous state in which it is at the present time. In the first case confronting this amendment a judge may well conclude that he will accept a majority decision. Another judge in another jurisdiction may decide that he will not do so. There is no law which determines which judge would be right. Now, when we are passing an amendment to this particular section, is the time to remove any doubt and this is the place in which to do it. We in the legislature should not leave any doubt existent when we have an opportunity of removing it. I think the remarks made by the hon. member for Welland are appropriate and that they bear out and confirm what I myself sought to indicate earlier.

It seems to me that this clause as originally drafted was quite plain and quite clear until the hon. member for Essex East offered his amendment. I think he has muddied the waters sufficiently to have created a great deal of difficulty. I suggest that the hon. member for Essex East in offering this amendment has completely misconceived the function of the jury. From time immemorial the function of the jury has been, in the words of the charge they receive, to try and make true deliverance between our sovereign lady, the queen and the prisoner at the bar. Their duty is to ascertain from the evidence presented whether the accused is innocent or guilty. The effect of the amendment offered by my hon. friend will be to send the jury on a detour where they may, and in many cases probably will, lose sight of what is their main function. The amendment introduced by the hon. member is in fact an invitation to juries to compromise on their verdicts. It is a suggestion to a jury and I am sure they will accept it as a direction by a judge such as is contained in the charge by a judge when directing the jury as to what the law is and what the functions of a judge and jury are.
This amendment would have the effect of the jury being told: "If you are in difficulties; if you find that one or two of the jurymen are not prepared to go along with a verdict of guilty or are not prepared to go along with a verdict of not guilty, you can bring in a verdict of guilty and couple that with a recommendation for mercy at the appropriate time".
I say that should not be done at that time The jury should come to its verdict as tc guilt or innocence on the evidence, and then it is functus officio; their duty is completed. They may then be asked, after they have brought in their verdict on the issue of guilt or innocence, whether or not they wish to make any recommendation so far as clemency is concerned.
May I point out, Mr. Chairman, that I think my hon. friend, in dealing with this matter, laid the foundation of his argument mainly on the ground that there might be

Criminal Code
a divided jury. However, there are many instances which occur to me where other reasons would justify a jury making a recommendation for clemency after their verdict had been rendered.
Consider a case of insanity for example. I mentioned this when I spoke on second reading. The evidence offered to prove insanity may not be sufficient to bring it squarely within the M'Naghten rules. However, there may be sufficient evidence to indicate such a degree of mental defectiveness as will not justify a verdict of not guilty because of insanity, but which may put a jury in the position that, having brought in the verdict of guilty as they are required to do by law, when the opportunity is later offered to them they will say, "We think that on the strength of the evidence submitted we are perfectly justified and it is perfectly proper for us to bring in this recommendation for clemency".
I can think of a case of provocation. Under certain circumstances provocation justifies a verdict of manslaughter. I can think of many cases where there might be provocation and the provocation may be grave. Then, having suffered the provocation, the accused might go and secure a weapon and come back and commit the crime of murder. Then there would be those elements of preparation and planning which are essential to prove a charge of capital murder as defined in this bill.
The jury might decide that while the preparation and planning, which were incidental to the offence, did not permit them to find the accused not guilty of capital murder, after having brought in the verdict of guilty and when asked this question by the judge they might say "We feel we should make a recommendation for clemency".
I can think of a case of two young boys, one of whom is a few weeks under the age at which sentence of death can be pronounced upon him and the other just a few weeks over that age. Surely a jury, in those circumstances, having fulfilled their duty and having brought in a verdict of guilty of capital murder might, when invited by the judge under the terms of this clause, feel there should be a recommendation for mercy because they feel it is wrong that one man should have his life spared and the other should suffer the penalty of death.
Those are some circumstances which could justify recommendation for clemency, but they should not be brought in at the same time as the main verdict; they should be considered as matters completely extraneous to the main issue, which is that of guilt or innocence. Once that has been decided, then and then only should the jury consider this question of clemency. For this reason, Mr. 
Chairman, I must say that I cannot in any way support the amendment introduced by the hon. member.
