Mr. Chairman, this is the third time I have risen to speak to clause 13. I do not apologize for rising again.
I do not think we can differentiate between the principle of clause 13 and the amendment. I raised a number of points both on the section as originally drafted and on the amendment and I am not going to cover that ground again. However, during the dinner recess I had the opportunity of looking into this clause and the amendment in more detail and I should like to ask, before a vote is taken on the amendment or on the clause as originally drafted, if we could hear the Minister of Justice's views on what I think is a rather important point.
Under the clause as contained in this bill we have the situation where after a jury find a person guilty the judge puts a certain question to them and asks whether they have any recommendation to make with regard to clemency. Under the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Essex East we have the recommendation for a change which means the two questions shall be put at the same time in the charge of the judge to the jury.
This leads me to a major matter of principle and a question which I hope the Minister of Justice will see fit to answer. My point is this. I still feel that basically, in principle, both clause 13 as contained in the bill introduced by the Minister of Justice and the amendment moved by my hon. friend are the same. However, I should like to ask the Minister of Justice this question. This is based on the law of California and a number of other states in which the jury has a definite say as to the penalty. Under the law of California and many other states the decision of the jury has a definite bearing upon the penalty.
Three times this afternoon the Minister of Justice stated that the penalty should be set forth in the statute. I hope I am not misinterpreting the statement of the minister, and I agree with what he said. The Minister of Justice nods his head, so apparently he thinks I have put the correct interpretation on his words.
The principle of clause 13 and the amendment give the jury, either before or after reaching their verdict, depending upon whether you take the clause in the bill or in the amendment, certain authority. Since six o'clock I have had an opportunity of looking at the speech made by the Prime Minister. I must say that I feel if one reads the comment of the Prime Minister as found on page 5528 of Hansard there can only be

one inference taken from that statement. The minister will find the statement at the bottom of that page. The inference is that a recommendation for mercy by a jury is one which must receive the most serious and moral consideration of the governor general in council. I can therefore understand from reading that one sentence why the press interpreted it as meaning that a recommendation for mercy from the jury would mean commutation of the death sentence to life imprisonment.
I should like to ask the minister if he can tell this committee what is the end result of clause 13, bearing in mind his contention that the penalty should be provided by law and the fact that this clause, even with the amendment, is based in principle on the statutory law of California. Why should the Minister of Justice reject the idea of prescribing in law that when there is no recommendation from the jury it means the death sentence unless the royal prerogative of clemency is exercised, and that recommendations of clemency would automatically mean the commutation of death sentences to life imprisonment?
The minister knows that this is the law in many states and, in principle, clause 13 even as amended means the same. I think this is an important matter and I hope the minister will see fit to explain why, since he has followed certain statutes in the south so closely, he has not carried this idea to its completion by making the penalty depend on the decision of the jury.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: In approaching this problem we reached the conclusion that the jury should have one primary task, that is, to determine whether or not an accused person is guilty as charged. The verdict may be varied, of course; a man may be found not guilty of murder, but guilty of manslaughter and so on. But we feel the jury should be in a position where they can approach this awesome task without their minds being burdened by consideration of whether or not they themselves are to be in the position of determining what penalty the accused should pay. We think the jury should not have to determine that question.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: You are doing it under clause 13.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
No. If the hon. member will bear with me, I will endeavour to explain to him why not. We think the jury should pass on the question of fact, whether or not the accused is guilty of the charge for which he stands trial. That is all, up to this point, that they are required to determine and they are entitled to be placed in a position where they
Criminal Code
may make that determination without having at the same time to take into account the consequence of their verdict. Therefore we have endeavoured in the legislation to isolate this task as far as it can be isolated.
I am not suggesting for a moment that jurymen are not human beings and that they have no knowledge of the law but in so far as the law imposes on them the duty of ascertaining whether or not a person is guilty or innocent they are entitled so far as it can be provided to bring in that decision without being distracted by extraneous consideration.
Having done that, they are then asked, in accordance with clause 13 now under consideration, to say whether or not they think the accused, whom they have found guilty, should be shown clemency-whether they think any recommendations should be made in this respect. We have deliberately separated the two processes, the two tasks, if you like, which we are imposing on the jury.
For reasons I gave before six o'clock we think it would be improper to invite anyone to place before the jury at the time they retire to consider their verdict the question of whether or not their considerations in reaching a verdict should be clouded by the question of mercy. To do so would certainly be placing upon jurymen a perplexing task. Some members of the jury might be inclined to acquittal. Those who were inclined to a verdict of guilty could say to them, if the amendment of the hon. member for Essex East were adopted: never mind about holding out; let us get together and agree because even if we do convict the judge has told us we can bring in a recommendation for mercy; so let us convict and bring in a recommendation for mercy; if you will agree to convict we shall agree to support a recommendation. Thus the simple question of guilt or innocence would be clouded with these other considerations.
That is why we have thought it esential to keep these two questions apart and for the jury to consider them entirely separately. It is only after a jury has found an accused person guilty of capital murder that they are invited or instructed by the judge that they may, if they wish, bring in a recommendation. The jury will then retire and reach a decision on that point. This being the system we have devised and incorporated into this bill I must beg to differ with the hon. member for Vancouver East when he says it is based on Californian statutes. It is not. Under that system, if I read it correctly, the jury which tries the issue of facts is also charged with the ultimate decision as to what should be the penalty, that is, whether

Criminal Code
the penalty should be death or life imprisonment. If the hon. member has followed me thus far he will appreciate we have not adopted that practice.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: That is my question. Why have you not adopted it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: I am coming to that. We have imposed on the jury the responsibility of determining guilt or innocence and then we have made clear in our law that they have the right to bring in a recommendation. I am sure my hon. friends will appreciate that the recommendation is only a recommendation and is not binding. We have done this deliberately because we felt that the law itself should provide the penalty in respect of an issue as supremely important as life or death, and it is not right to impose upon the same 12 men, who have had the responsibility of determining the guilt or innocence of an accused, the responsibility of saying whether that accused shall pay the death penalty or shall be subject to a lesser penalty. We feel the law should provide that, and that legislators should say that. I do not know whether or not my hon. friends will agree with that.

speechtext:
No. The simple issue before a jury involves the question of guilt or innocence. That is the only issue which we feel

can appropriately be placed before the jury as a matter for their final and ultimate determination.
With respect to the law of California, if I read it correctly, it provides that the trier of fact shall fix the penalty. Therefore, the jury, being the body to try the fact, as to guilt or innocence, under the provisions of California law must fix the penalty in accordance with its verdict.
I am not sure that my hon. friends will agree with me, but I can only say again that we have considered this very carefully and have rejected that approach. We felt that it is not proper, fair, nor indeed appropriate to the jury system to have the same twelve men who are asked to decide this awful question -awful in the proper sense of the word-this awesome question as to whether a man is guilty or not of a charge of capital murder, then to go on and decide whether the man shall be hanged. I do not think that is a proper question to put to a jury. I think that is a responsibility of the legislators; that is, to say whether or not a person found guilty of capital murder shall hang, and that is what we are inviting this committee to provide.
The issue before the jury is then simple. It is simple but is awesome, and it is the only proper responsibility to impose upon the jury -deciding whether a man is guilty of capital murder or not. The jury having decided that question, it is our feeling that the law should provide the penalty. Then, as outlined in clause 13 of this bill, the jury is asked subsequently-not as part of a mixed bag to be considered at the same time-whether or not it wishes to make a recommendation for or against mercy, and it makes that recommendation without regard to the guilt or innocence of the accused because that issue has been settled.
My friend, the hon. member for Peace River, has posed the sort of consideration that we think proper to put to the jury. A jury may have found a man guilty of capital murder because it found that the technical defence of provocation, which would have absolved the accused from guilt, was not fully established. Perhaps a mounting series of provocations and irritations occurred and he finally succumbed to that provocation but instead of committing the murder immediately the individual went out and bought a gun and 24 hours later, or in some cases, with a few hours' intervention, committed the offence. In that event the law is such that the defence of provocation is not available to the accused, yet members of the jury might feel, as I have said to the committee earlier, there but for the grace of God go I; I should have done the same thing had I been subject to the same considerations,

provocations and irritations; I should not have been strong enough to stand up against them. That jury cannot avoid finding the man guilty of a planned and deliberate murder but, when and if it is asked whether it recommends clemency, certainly the members of that jury will recommend mercy. I do not feel that these issues will arise often, but they will arise, and when they arise they will be most extraordinarily difficult issues to resolve.
I should now like to come to what my hon. friend said about the Prime Minister's speech. I have read his speech again very carefully and believe what he really said was that when the jury that has tried the issue has come to its decision, and when that jury of the accused's peers states that under the circumstances it recommends the exercise of clemency, the cabinet is bound to be profoundly influenced by that recommendation. However, it is still only a recommendation. It is on that basis we have placed it in the provisions which are now before the committee.
The issue now before us in a sense is an issue which is comparatively simple: on the one hand, should the question regarding the jury's recommendation be put before the jury for its consideration at the same time they are considering the question of guilt or innocence? That is the suggestion of my friend the hon. member for Essex East. On the other hand, should the question be put to the jury only after it has considered the question of guilt or innocence and after the jury has decided it was bound to bring in a verdict of guilty? That is our suggestion, as incorporated into this bill.
For the reasons I have given, while respecting fully the views and arguments that have been advanced, I cannot accept them. I think the adoption of that practice would place juries in an intolerable position, requiring them to consider two issues at once. Therefore, I am unable to accept the amendment.
I think perhaps I should suggest, without getting into that area which you, Mr. Chairman, have said should be discussed separately, with which statement I thoroughly agree, regarding the question of whether the recommendation should be unanimous, that my hon. friends ought to look at the question which is to be put to the jury:
Do you wish to make any recommendation as to whether or not he should be granted clemency?
Having asked that question, the judge will then state the following:
You are not required to make any recommendation but if you do make a recommendation either in favour of clemency or against it, your recommendation will be included in the report that I am
Criminal Code
required to make of this case to the Minister of Justice and will be given due consideration.
In effect the jury will have three alternatives. The jury will be able to say that it has a recommendation to make for clemency; that it has a recommendation to make against clemency; or that it does not wish to make or is unable to agree in respect of a recommendation. It seems to me, those being the three clear alternatives that we place before the jury by the form of the question, that all the issues and all the variations of the issue which are in the minds of the hon. members are properly reflected in that question which the jury will be asked.
In conclusion, I would say it seems to me that the proposal as we have placed it before the committee in the form of clause 13 of this bill is a desirable one because it removes from the realm of uncertainty and places in the realm of absolute certainty the question of whether or not the jury is entitled to make a recommendation, but it places that question before the jury at the proper time, namely after they have reached their verdict on the question of guilty or not guilty.

Mr. Chairman, as a layman I have listened very carefully to the arguments of the Minister of Justice. I realize that this is a technical, legal and intangible problem which is being discussed by persons on both sides of the house who are trying to face it quite honestly. But the point that bothered me when the Minister of Justice was speaking if I heard him correctly, was that he said that juries must not be clouded by considerations of mercy. That struck me rather hard because I am of the opinion that juries should always be terrified by considerations of mercy. I could not quite go along with him in that respect.
In dealing with a problem in which there is such, shall I say, hairline differences between the proponents of one point of view and of

Criminal Code
the other I always come down on the side of mercy. I think it is quite true to say in this instance that the hon. member for Essex East, the hon. member for Niagara Falls and the member for Kootenay West are three minds that think alike. Therefore, I am of the opinion that if there is a sort of technical difference of opinion the committee would be wise to pass legislation about which the opinion of any juror would be clouded with considerations of mercy. I should like to make a few remarks with respect to the last comments by the Minister of Justice. In the first place, it was suggested by the minister that it might be possible in a trial for capital murder for

the jury to escape any consideration of the penalty. I suggest to the minister that this is absolutely not possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: I think the hon. lady will realize I did say that the jurymen are human beings and therefore it will not be possible for them completely to divorce their minds from it. We felt that in so far as the law could do it, it should endeavour to make it possible.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
I accept this explanation, and it is what the minister said previously. But it cannot be possible for them to escape the fact that they are asked to decide two things. The first is whether the man is guilty of capital murder. No Canadian will be able to escape the necessary knowledge that when a man is guilty of this crime it will mean that in all probability he will be hanged. Therefore this very consideration is one which necessarily bears in upon their minds and consciences, namely the fact that in all likelihood when they find that the answer to this question is yes the man will meet his Maker as a result of the due process of law.
Second, the minister has suggested that it is difficult for a jury to dissociate the two things in their minds, one, guilt or innocence, and, two, the penalty. I am sure the minister knows-and I can speak only for the province of Ontario-that in any civil action where there is a jury there are two issues to be tried. One is the equivalent of guilt or innocence, namely fault or not of the defendant; and, two, if there is fault, what is the measure of damages? Now, in my experience of the law in the province of Ontario all jurors have been sufficienly able to differentiate between these two individual problems as to decide them independently one of the other. I suggest to the minister that juries are no less capable of doing this where the two problems which they must resolve are, one, guilt or innocence on the count of capital murder; and, two, the punishment which is to be meted out; and that this may be decided in one deliberation but in two stages. Certainly I would suggest that if a jury is expected to be as sophisticated as the amendment now before this committee will require it to be-and I think the hon. member for Essex East has already pointed this out- there are six different judgments, six different verdicts, which may be given on a charge of capital murder. If they can navigate among the intricacies of these six possible results, then I say to the minister they can separate in their minds the two things.
If there is one thing that has impressed me in my short experience in the law, it is the tremendous consideration which ordinary Canadians from every walk of life give to

a capital crime. Their attention never wanders either from the directions of the judge or the representations made by counsel or the evidence of the witnesses. They never miss a word. They direct themselves with the most astonishing clarity of mind to the decision they are asked to make. In my opinion they are a shining example of the best things in any community because they address themselves to the issue and solely to the issue.
If this is so, and it has been proven to be so, I suggest in all humility to the minister that the jurors are able to decide these two issues at the one time and that they should decide them at the one time rather than at separate times. They should not be called upon to make a second crucial decision when a period of time has intervened from the making of their first decision and knowing that when they brought in their first verdict finding the accused guilty of capital murder he died a little then and his family and, indeed, his counsel, also died a little. They should not be asked to retire again to make up their minds knowing that while they are out there will be great anguish on the part of the accused and everyone else in the courtroom and also knowing that if they come back and recommend against clemency, something that has never happened in our criminal law, they will be on the spot again and the accused, his family and friends and, indeed, members of the public, will die a little more. I would ask the minister and other hon. members to address themselves most seriously to this matter before voting on the amendment because it is of crucial importance. Those of us who practice in the defence of those who are accused but not proven to be guilty of a capital crime ask that fair treatment be accorded by having the jury charged as to this matter before they deliberate at all and not, as proposed in the legislation, after they have found the accused guilty of the offence.

Mr. Chairman, I find it necessary to rise tonight to speak in support of the Minister of Justice and against the amendment on two or three grounds. May I say that I speak as one who has served as a juror. I have sat on panels which have had to administer justice and I know the heart-throbs that men and women who go through this experience have.
With all due deference to the hon. member for Niagara Falls, I say that in my opinion jurors have one main task, to determine first of all the guilt or innocence of the accused. Once the jurors have done that they are free, as provided in clause 13, to offer some suggestions with respect to clemency. I am quite sure that jurors in a murder trial will have a much closer view of the
Criminal Code
actual case than anyone else, and I would be quite prepared to listen to any argument by a jury with respect to clemency after the verdict has been rendered. After all, those who are summoned to serve on these panels are first of all asked one question. Is the accused innocent or guilty? My stand on capital punishment is very well known in this house. I somehow feel we are straying too far into the path of mercy. We are becoming too benevolent. Mr. Chairman, I raised another question with regard to this clause and the comments that I made were supported by the hon. member for Welland. It had to do with whether or not a majority would be sufficient or whether the rule of unanimity would apply. What would happen in the event of one juryman, let us say, being against a recommendation for clemency and the other eleven being in favour. The point was made that unless this ambiguity was resolved this question would arise, that is that there would be different attitudes taken by different judges, and the law would not become settled. There is ambiguity in the very language of the section and so it is our responsibility now to remove it.
If the minister takes the position that he believes the jury must, as in the case of a determination of guilt, be unanimous, then let him say so. If that is the position, let him put it in the statute. However, we take the position that the question is now doubtful, that it is not at all settled and that it is one that should be settled. I should be grateful for the minister's reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
I recognize the fact that this is a difficult question. However, I must start from the premise that we are asking here a question on a recommendation of the jury. The judge is going to ask the jury whether they have any recommendation to make. I therefore suggest that it would be a mistake to import into the law any provision which suggests that the jury can be less than unanimous. It must be borne in mind that the provision for unanimity is, generally speaking, one that works in favour of the accused. I therefore think it is proper that we should expect the same principle to be carried forward with respect to their recommendation which is now under consideration. The judge is not addressing this question to the jurors individually. He is addressing it to the jury collectively and he is asking them as a jury whether they wish to make any recommendation first, whether the accused should be granted clemency; and second, whether the accused should not be granted clemency. Then, as I said a moment ago, that actually and necessarily imports three alternatives. The jury may say, "Yes, we recommend that he should be granted clemency" or "We recommend that he should not be granted clemency" or "We are unable or do not wish to make any recommendation". I think that is all the jury should be invited to do.
I would point out that the judge, if he wishes to do so, may examine the jury as to the state of their minds. The judge is obligated by the provisions of the statute, section 643, to make a report of the case to the

Minister of Justice for the information of the governor in council. I have thought of this matter a great deal both before I introduced the bill and since then, and also since this discussion started, but on reflection I would not be prepared to introduce into the law anything which would suggest to the jury that they may be less than unanimous. On the other hand, however, I would not be prepared to introduce into the law anything which would suggest that the judge may not report to the Minister of Justice unless the jury says "Our verdict is unanimous".
I have tried earnestly to devise an amendment that would meet these problems but I may say quite frankly that I have not been able to devise one which would not directly suggest to the jury that they may make a compromise decision, and I think this would be an unfortunate thing to suggest to the jury. I recognize the fact that juries may not be able to agree upon a recommendation. Indeed, juries on occasion have been unable to agree on a verdict. However, this is a very undesirable thing. It is a thing to be avoided and to be done only as a last resort. I therefore think it would be a mistake to write into the law anything that would suggest to the jury that they may be less than unanimous.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: The minister has stated his position quite clearly, I think, in so far as his objective is concerned of having the jury treated as a unit. However, that does not really resolve the question. Suppose that, after the judge reads out this particular provision, the jury repairs to the jury room, to bring in a verdict of guilty and then come back and the foreman of the jury says to the judge, "We understand the rule of unanimity as far as guilt is concerned and we the jury have found this individual guilty of murder. However we cannot agree on whether or not there should be a recommendation of clemency. Two of us take the position that there should not be such a recommendation and ten of us take the position that there should be one. May we now bring in such a recommendation?" What is the judge going to say?

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY

I think the judge would then be in the same position that he is in with respect to the verdict of the jury. As far as I can ascertain

and I have asked my officers to consider this matter-there is in the law no clear and specific provision which says in so many words that the jury's verdict must be unanimous. We are looking further.

No. Section 560 states that where the judge is satisfied that no further

purpose would be served by keeping a jury in an attempt to have it arrive at a unanimous verdict, he may discharge the jury. It is true that by implication the verdict must be unanimous but it is not specifically stated. However, the practice has grown up that where the jury shows quite clearly that it is not able to arrive at a unanimous verdict, the judge dismisses the jury and that trial is nugatory. The inability of the jury to agree on a recommendation would not make the trial nugatory. What would happen then, as I see it, is quite clear. The judge would simply report that after so much deliberation as was necessary it became quite apparent that the jury were unable to agree on a recommendation. He might indeed have elicited from the jury the extent of their disagreement; and I am satisfied that in the discharge of his statutory duty he would report to the Minister of Justice the extent of the disagreement. Then the facts of the situation would be clearly outlined to the governor in council for his guidance. After all, the purpose of this recommendation is for the guidance of the governor in council. If therefore the jury reach a unanimous decision that they should recommend mercy, that fact is reported by the judge. If they should reach a unanimous decision that they should not recommend mercy, it is also reported. If after such deliberation and return to the judge for further instructions as may be necessary, it becomes perfectly clear that they cannot reach a decision one way or another, that fact is also reported. I do not think that we can do more or that we should do more. To do more would involve the suggestion that a decision of the jury should be less than unanimous. If we cannot get a decision, then the effect of the section is that that fact will be reported to the Minister of Justice and it will then be obvious to the governor in council that some favoured mercy and some did not favour mercy.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
I do not wish to repeat the argument for something less than unanimity except to say this. I believe the minister has treated this point as one of primary substance when it is not one of primary concern. The primary question is the question of whether the accused is guilty or not guilty. Whether or not there should be a recommendation for clemency is not of the same order or category as the main decision; but the minister speaks of the jury, without speaking in terms of majority or minority, both in terms of unanimity with regard to guilt and unanimity with regard to recommendation.
I suggest to the minister the following. The purpose of this clause, I take it, is not to create a new procedure, a new tradition, or
Criminal Code
in fact really to create new law. The purpose of this clause is to bring home to juries an assumed power which they have had, I suppose, ever since our jury system in capital cases was established. I say this because now, although the law is not at all explicit, juries bring in recommendations for clemency, not in every instance but in so many cases where there is not even any suggestion by the court that they should do so.
That being the case I suggest to the minister that his reluctance to meet the point the hon. member for Welland and others have put will mean that juries will do the very thing I have suggested. Juries will not be able to agree in some instances, and the foreman of the jury will say, "Some of us believe there should be a recommendation for mercy; three of us think there should not, but the rest think there should".
The Minister of Justice, notwithstanding his objective of maintaining the jury as a unanimous body, will be faced I think by a practice which will not be denied under the law as it is to be amended or under the practice which is now followed.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I indicated earlier that I was in many ways very much opposed to the amendment contained in clause 13, but at this time I should like to limit my remarks to the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Welland, which I believe has a great deal of merit, especially when one reads the clause as phrased.
This clause will create many doubts about things which possibly it was the intention of the officer who drafted the clause to clarify. I should like to comment on some of the remarks made by the Minister of Justice a moment ago intending to indicate to the committee that the intention behind this clause was to ascertain that the finding of guilt and the recommendation for mercy would not become two instruments of battle among jurymen.
Certainly if the Minister of Justice meant this seriously he should realize that the clause as phrased does exactly the opposite of what he had in mind. I say this because if it was the intention to enact a clause which would give absolute freedom to jurymen with regard to clemency and it was not to be coupled with the discussion as to guilt, the minister should have said so. But in this clause the minister makes it necessary for jurymen to discuss their recommendation with regard to clemency at the same time as they discuss their finding of guilty or not guilty.
All the jurymen must find in favour of clemency to make such a recommendation, or they must unanimously decide against making any such recommendation. Therefore this clause takes away the right of some

Criminal Code
jurymen to vote against clemency and means they will possibly be urged by the other jurymen to go into the question of the accused being not guilty because they cannot obtain a bargaining point and this matter has to be decided unanimously.
Therefore although I am not in favour of this clause dealing with a recommendation for clemency becoming part of our statutes, if it is included in the statute it should be left to the discretion of each and every member of the jury to indicate his wish. It could be indicated to the judge that four jurymen were in favour of recommending clemency and so many others were against it and so on. I feel there is much merit in that suggestion.
If the Minister of Justice will read the clause itself, the first paragraph seems to indicate that the question should be asked of each and every juryman and not of the jury as a whole. The first paragraph of the clause says:
Where a jury finds an accused guilty of an offence punishable by death, the judge who presides at the trial shall, before discharging the jury, put to them the following question:
If that were meant to mean the jury as a body, the words would be "put to it". If you are going to put the question to "them" you must foresee that you will get an answer from each and every one, and not from the jury as a body.
Later on in the clause the question of whether or not there is a recommendation for clemency is dealt with. How can the jury vote on this matter? They either want clemency or they do not, and they have to vote "yes" or "no". In these circumstances how could they report to the judge that they absolutely do not wish to recommend clemency? It sems to me that this phraseology means it is the intention to obtain from each and every juryman his opinion or disposition with regard to this matter, "Are you in favour of clemency or not?". If this is the intention, why not make the words very clear? It is not a vote; it is not a determination; it is a recommendation in favour of or against clemency.
Surely if it is a matter of a vote of all the jurymen, the vote should be that they favour a recommendation for clemency or they do not. How can you recommend that no clemency be given? You can be against recommending clemency, but certainly you cannot in the same vote decide that no recommendation for clemency shall be made.
I see a slight distinction there. However, I am quite sure that if the minister reads that first paragraph again it will indicate to him that the intention of this clause is to have the question put to each and every juryman. Although I am against the question being

included in our statute, I agree that if it is included there is a great deal of merit in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Welland. If it is a matter of recommendation the complete opinion of the men who sat on the jury should be given to the judge. If so many are in favour of recommending clemency and so many are against it, those figures should at least be given. It should be so written in the act, so that the judge will have a clear and definite picture of the jury's intention in deciding the course he is to follow.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can, I regret, only say again that the jury is here being invited to make a recommendation; it is not being invited to reach a verdict. It is to my mind quite clear that if they are unable to agree, that fact will be reported to the judge and will be included by him in his report to the Minister of Justice.
The experience is that judges make very full reports on these cases and I have no doubt that the opinion or the state of mind of the jury will be ascertained by the judge and reported to the minister. Then it will be reported by the minister to the cabinet. But if what the jury is asked to do is make a recommendation, if they can make a recommendation they will make one as a jury. If they are unable to arrive at a recommendation they will report as much to the judge. Since they are only asked for a recommendation, it seems to me that it is a perfectly satisfactory state of affairs.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
I do not think this clause should be carried before I have a chance to outline the ridiculous position in which our judges would be placed in a number of instances should this provision be enacted. If a jury finds a man guilty of murder and decides to make a recommendation for clemency the judge is placed in the ridiculous position of having to go to his room, return with his black gloves and tricorne and everything else before sentencing the accused to death, knowing full well that in most cases the sentence will be commuted because of the jury's recommendation.
I am sure most judges would be reluctant to take part in what I would term to be a comedy. It is not good for justice that a man should be sentenced to death when we know full well-and the words of the Prime Minister leave no room for any other interpretation-that in most of these cases where clemency has been asked by the jury the sentence will not be carried out. I can imagine that in such cases the lawyer will say to his client, "Do not worry; we have a recommendation for clemency. This is only for fun; the sentence will never be carried out". This is something we should bear in mind before this clause is carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: The hon. member's concern for the situation of the judges would carry a good deal more weight if I did not know for a fact that many judges place themselves in the position which the hon. member has described, because at the present time it is far from rare that a judge who, following a verdict of guilty from a jury has solemnly donned the black cap and sentenced the accused to death, yet recommends in his report to the Minister of Justice that mercy should be shown. So I do not think the hon. member need have any fear about judges being placed in a ridiculous position. The judges themselves are, frequently, not reluctant to express their views for such guidance to the governor in council as may be attached to them with respect to whether or not mercy may be shown, notwithstanding that the jury had brought in a verdict of guilty and that they themselves had pronounced the death sentence.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: I do not want to pursue this point at length, but I think the minister himself must be aware of the criticism made by many judges in this country when death sentences which they have imposed have been commuted. I think that when we are trying to introduce a new concept of law dealing with the death penalty we should endeavour at the same time to find a system which would avoid such circumstances as I have described.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: If there be anything wrong with this situation I can only say that in some cases it is created by the judges themselves inasmuch as they make recommendations of their own notwithstanding the verdict of the jury. What we are doing here is clearing up an uncertainty in the law, namely, whether or not the jury has the right to make recommendations. That is the main purpose of this clause. The legislation provides means of establishing in the minds of juries that they have this right if they wish to exercise it and that their recommendations will be reported to the Minister of Justice. This is no great departure, seen in its proper prospective. It merely makes clear that the jury has the right to make such a recommendation. At the moment there is some doubt about it.

As I indicated a moment ago when I made some observations about what had been said by the hon. member for Welland, I have something more to say about this particular clause, clause 13. I trust I shall have the support of many members of this committee in my efforts to ascertain that this clause is not passed and shall not be placed on our statute books.

The Minister of Justice indicated that judges will not be embarrassed if there is a recommendation to mercy-that they will don the black cap and pronounce sentence notwithstanding. But what cap will the cabinet wear when it considers one of these recommendations to mercy; what gown will it put on and under what terms will it make a choice between death and life imprisonment? I am sure members of this committee are entitled to ask the Minister of Justice these questions. We know that throughout history statutes have been made pertaining to royal prerogatives. They have always been used to limit them, not to enlarge them. This statute, however, will be a procedure to enlarge the royal prerogative of mercy. I realize it is fitting that such a recourse should be in existence. I consider it to be a great and extraordinary thing, and in my opinion it should remain thus. It should not be placed in the hands of politicians as the product of a statute. This clause means placing into the hands of politicians final responsibility in the matter of capital punishment in this country and to that I am absolutely opposed.
No one who knows something about the confusion which this clause can bring about has failed to support my views on this matter. We know that recommendations, if they have any value, will be made by juries in certain areas. The government is the government of all Canada. We know that possibly it will become known that in certain areas juries will commonly bring in recommendations for mercy-recommendations which are invariably followed by the politicians. How can citizens be assured that justice will be done if politicians have the final decision on a matter of this grave importance?

speechtext: I wonder if I may ask the hon. member a question? Does he not think that the setting up of different categories of murder will lead to fewer cases coming before the cabinet for consideration, and does this not mean that the use of the royal prerogative will be reduced rather than extended?

I am speaking on behalf of those individuals who should like to see justice done by our courts. That is why I voted in favour of the principle of this bill. That principle involves an attempt to indicate to our courts, judges and juries, what constitutes the offence of murder to be punished by death, and what constitutes the other types of murder, punishable by life imprisonment only. It is only in respect of the determination of the gravity of the crime which should be contained in this bill. It should be set forth clearly for the guidance of the judges and jury in determining what constitutes a

Criminal Code
crime which is punishable by death, and a non-capital crime, although murder, punishable by life imprisonment. That decision should rest with the judges and juries in this country and not be placed into the hands of the politicians and crown employees.
I am speaking in regard to clause 1 because I feel that clause 13 is coupled with the other clauses of the bill. I find it very odd that we should concern ourselves with the fine distinctions which we have attempted to make between capital and non-capital murder.
As the bill is now proposed, I suggest the police officers, the crown prosecutors, and other employees in the field of justice will make the decisions as to whether an offence is capital murder or non-capital murder. I say that is absolutely wrong. I suggest that our courts, judges and juries should decide what crime an accused individual is guilty of, and that the penalty should be provided by legislation.
I should like to suggest that in certain cases there will be doubt as to why an individual was charged with a non-capital murder which carries only a sentence of life imprisonment. There might very well be talk of the fact that a man has contributed $10,000 in order to protect his son, following which a charge of non-capital murder was laid.

I object to this proposed clause 13 because of the flimsy recommendations which our judges will now ask our juries to make in regard to capital and non-capital murder, which involves an element of distinction which is not properly defined, and which could result in different applications of the law in different parts of the country. I trust the hon. member understood that.
I suggest the law is clear today and that we should retain that clarity in respect of the distinctions which are proposed by this bill. This is a distinction provided by this bill to permit our judges and juries to make findings appropriate to specific circumstances. I am not in favour of introducing a procedure which will bring about the uncertainty of the application of this measure. My great fear is not so much what recommendations we may have from different localities. That difficulty may be overcome. What I am concerned with is what is the cabinet to do with the recommendations? Is the Minister of Justice prepared to say that when there is a recommendation from a jury which comes from the area where the crime was committed that the cabinet is entitled to disregard it and not commute the sentence? What will the cabinet do in other instances? Why make the cabinet the court of appeal, as this clause does? Why not give the authority to the judge and jury, those people who have been called in to decide the case on behalf of the citizens or the locality? Why place the cabinet in the position of being the court of appeal? I am sure that this cabinet, or any other cabinet, will regret it for a long time if clause 13, which we are now discussing, passes and is placed in the Criminal Code.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question. Do we gather from what he has said that he is unalterably opposed to any final authority in so far as the prerogative of mercy is concerned?

speechtext:
I thought I made that clear. I am not opposed to the royal prerogative. At the present time I am not discussing the royal prerogative. If there is the head of a country, then it is fitting that we give to
Criminal Code
that authority the right to pardon. This is a part of our society, something which we consider in the development of our social structure and of our democratic way of life as being most fitting. But should we add to this prerogative? By many statutes we have limited the prerogatives of the crown in Canada. We have done this and it was fitting that we should do it. But why increase that prerogative and make it a matter of statute law as we are doing here by way of a recommendation for royal mercy? I say it is the wrong thing to do. It is a backward step for any government to take. I hope I have answered my hon. friend.
Royal mercy should remain an extraordinary thing that a citizen can resort to in special circumstances and possibly obtain it or try to obtain it. To implement it by way of a statute I say is wrong. I trust I have made it clear to my hon. friend that I am not opposed to the right itself which is a beautiful and a wonderful thing and ought to be used on extraordinary occasions. But I do not want to see it any every day matter, nor do I want to see it used as a court of appeal in murder cases.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
There is just one point in connection with this clause that bothers me a little bit, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Nickel Belt has raised the question of what purpose is to be served by this final recommendation. He has implied that the only use it could be put to would be to guide the cabinet in exercising the royal prerogative.
The jury is charged with two separate duties. One is to find whether the person is guilty or not of the charge of capital murder. Well, in that case, on the basis of evidence, an objective decision can be arrived at; but when it comes to consideration of making a decision on the second question, namely whether or not a recommendation for clemency should be made, I doubt very much whether a jury is in the same position with regard to making an objective decision because we all know from what we have seen take place in this house on more than one occasion when this question has come up that our views on it are fairly representative of those of the people of Canada and we know that just as we are divided in this house into two groups, one in favour of abolition and the other in favour of retention of capital punishment, so a jury must also have these two positions represented in it. I say this because a jury will have members who have come to the conclusion that capital punishment should be abolished. I feel sure that this will colour their judgment and they will not

Criminal Code
be as objective in bringing in a decision on whether or not there should be clemency as there would be in making a decision as to the guilt or innocence of the accused.
If you are not going to have an objective decision-and I do not think you are-I think because of that fact there will be an effort made to try and get on the jury a number of people who are in favour of abolition so that it can be pretty certain that there will always be a recommendation for clemency. There may be ways of getting over this. I never served on a jury. I do not know whether or not jurors are frequently challenged, but certainly there is this problem of whether you are going to get an objective decision. If this clause is meant to serve a useful purpose, then we should try to improve it and do everything possible to make sure that an objective decision will be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think every committee or commission that has considered the question of the exercise of the royal prerogative of mercy has come to the conclusion that it is not possible, if indeed it were desirable, that it should be exercised in accordance with a strict body of law and precedent.
May I just refer my hon. friend to one or two passages from the report of our own joint parliamentary committee, upon which, if I recall rightly, he himself served, when it was dealing with this subject. I will read from paragraph 12 on page 5 of the report:
Since each case is judged on its own merits, the practice governing remission cannot be reduced to a statement of settled principles. The decision in many cases necessitates a review of varying circumstances and, not infrequently, the weighing of conflicting considerations.. It would defeat the purpose of the exercise of the prerogative of mercy to attempt to codify the instances in which it might be invoked. The only safe and fair generalization than can be made is that commutation occurs in all cases where extenuating circumstances of a substantial nature exist or the degree of moral culpability is not sufficient to warrant the supreme penalty.
If these are the principles which are agreed on, and I wholeheartedly support that conclusion although I was not a member of the committee when it brought in its report, if it is agreed then that the considerations in the minds of the cabinet when it exercises the prerogative are many and varied and cannot be codified, then it does seem to me to be perfectly appropriate to say to the jury which has actually heard the evidence that you, too, will not be in a position to make any binding recommendation but of expressing an opinion whether or not there are present in this case the sort of facts which might warrant the suggestion that clemency be considered. This is why I feel, with deference to my hon. friend,

it is perfectly appropriate to say to these 12 men who, it is true, may exercise a judgment in making their recommendation based partly on their emotion, nevertheless what do you think about it, bearing in mind that there is first only a recommendation which is not binding.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: I thank the minister very much. He has clarified my problem quite a bit. If there were something in this clause which transferred what the minister quoted from the report which would sort of set down the principles on which that decision would be based, I think it would solve the problem. But there is nothing here. It simply says that they have to come to a decision whether or not they are going to recommend mercy, and on that basis alone I would think they would hardly be able to divorce their assessment of the evidence from their personal feelings as to capital punishment. That is the problem I was seeking to overcome.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, earlier the minister said that there would be no polling of the jury in open court in connection with a recommendation for mercy. Later he said the judge could ascertain what was in the minds of the jury by asking them. I think he said "them" and I understood him to be referring to the individual members of the jury. How can he do this without polling the jury?

speechtext: I was referring, of course, to what I had understood to be a suggestion made earlier that counsel would have the right to poll the jury. So far as I know the judge can ask the jury any question he wants in order to ascertain what may be their state of mind.

speechtext:
If I may return to what the minister said a moment ago, he said that the recommendation made as a result of the study in 1955 and 1956 was that the royal prerogative should remain free and there should be nothing to tie it down. I do not disagree with that in any way but in the light of that I fail to see how the minister could bring froward clause 13 if that was the guiding principle. Clause 13 introduces into the Criminal Code the very thing which will tie the hands of the cabinet in that they will be presented with a recommendation for mercy although it is not stated that they have to recommend mercy. But how could the procedure develop otherwise? In what other way could such a recommendation be treated? Is this not in a sense doing away with the liberty and freedom in respect of the use of the royal prerogative which the minister

has just indicated it was the recommendation of the committee that the cabinet should exercise?
I think the Minister of Justice is going contrary to the recommendation which he said is to be found in the report. He is tying the hands of the cabinet so that the royal prerogative will not be exercised in the free way in which it was before. The cabinet will be tied down by a recommendation which by law must be presented to it. That is the objection I have, and surely the Minister of Justice must realize that he is blowing hot and cold when he says that the purpose of implementing this clause is to retain freedom with regard to the use of the royal prerogative. I say it is quite clear that the procedure which will develop will not tend to retain freedom in the use of the royal prerogative but will limit it and make it susceptible to the tendencies of local juries. It will tie down the use of the royal prerogative to the attitude toward capital punishment that the cabinet may have from time to time. That is why I say that the very principle of freedom in the use of the royal prerogative to which the minister has referred is gravely limited by this clause.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must admit that this clause puzzles me a great deal. I should like to ask the minister to explain how and why he came to the decision to recommend this clause to the house. According to the explanation, its purpose is to enable the governor in council, in commuting a sentence of death, to direct that the prisoner shall not be released from the imprisonment to which the sentence is commuted without the prior approval of the governor in council.
The reason I say the clause puzzles me is that prior to this session when the Minister of Justice in his wisdom introduced major policy changes in the parole system of Canada and set up the national parole board this group in general and I in particular wholeheartedly supported the advance which the Minister of Justice recommended in our parole system. To the best of my knowledge the new parole board and system of parole have worked exceptionally well. As a matter of fact, I think the Minister of Justice can take a great deal of pride in the changes brought about in the last two years in the parole system.
90205-6-373
Criminal Code
However, under this clause the parole board and its authority are by-passed with respect to one type of criminal only. Although the board has done a terrific job in the last 18 months it is now by-passed because according to this clause the decision as to parole has to have the prior approval of the governor in council. I think the Minister of Justice knows that I have been interested in this question for many years. For the life of me I cannot conceive that the governor in council knows better than the parole board whether a man who was sentenced to death but has had his sentence commuted to life imprisonment is fit to be released into society or whether he should remain in jail for a number of years more or for the rest of his life. That is the function and purpose of the parole board. The whole function and purpose of the board involve undertaking a study of all prisoners. They study their history and the reports of the warden, the supervisor, the psychiatrist, the psychologist and so on. That is not a job that can be done by the governor in council.
With all the responsibilities that the governor in council has I would think the only understanding they could have with regard to a matter of this sort would be on the basis of information from the parole board. From where can such information come except from the parole board? Surely to heaven the members of the cabinet cannot make a detailed study of all the records, psychiatric and psychological reports and other reports. Of course not. That is why we have the parole board and that board has full power in every other offence involving penalties up to life imprisonment, offences such as rape, manslaughter and homicide without the death sentence. Such cases are the responsibility of the parole board but when it comes to just one type of case, that of the criminal sentenced to death who has had his sentence commuted to life imprisonment-

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: He committed a murder.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
All the others who commit non-capital murder and are sentenced to life imprisonment rather than capital punishment have also committed murder but they come under the parole board. As I read the clause, and I think I am right, when a sentence of death is commuted to life imprisonment that person cannot be granted parole without the consent of the governor in council.
I want it made very clear that I think extraordinary care must be taken that, whether it is 12 years or 50 years, if a man is not fit to be released in society, he should not be released, whether he is in jail for rape,

Criminal Code
homicide or any other reason such as punishment as a trafficker. What I cannot understand is why in this particular case the parole board, which is the only body that has knowledge of the matter, is by-passed in the final answer. In this situation the case must go before the governor in council.
I think the Minister of Justice understands why I am a little puzzled. I know he must have had some reason for putting in this provision. I think most of us in this chamber, being reasonable people, would be interested in knowing the reason. Men may be sentenced to life imprisonment for rape and other offences. Why is it that in this particular case the governor in council has the last say?
