speechtext: Does the minister wish to reply?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Yes. This clause is put in here for two reasons, really. First it must be remembered that the only persons whose sentence of death will be commuted to life imprisonment from now on will be, generally speaking, persons who the jury has decided committed a planned and deliberate killing. My hon. friend must bear in mind that this will be the situation from now on whereas it has not been the situation up to the present time. Up to the present time, all murder carried the death penalty and therefore everyone who committed murder and was convicted of murder would have his case come before the cabinet. Therefore all murderers were susceptible of having their sentences commuted to life imprisonment. From now on, however, the death penalty will be imposed only on those who are guilty of capital murder; that is to say on those who, the jury has found, have committed a planned and deliberate killing. Hence commutation, if it should take place, from now on is going to take place with respect to a man who has committed a planned or deliberate murder or, alternatively, who has killed in the course of the commission of a crime which itself imports the element of planning and deliberation.
The first point is that the type of crime which will now be coming forward for commutation will be a much more restricted one than the type of crime which has been subject to commutation in the past. However, there still may be commutation. We have discussed this matter quite fully already and I shall therefore not go into too much detail. However, let me remind my hon. friend of this fact. There may be this commutation although the verdict is guilty of planned and deliberate killing. For instance, in a case in which, although the man was not proved to be insane within the technical meaning of the law, psychiatrists' reports are such as to
[Mr. Winch.)
raise in the minds of the cabinet a doubt or a feeling that he is not a normally sane person, then in accordance with the well understood practice that we do not hang persons who are not mentally responsible, that man may have his sentence commuted although he has committed a particular type of crime and although he may be a type of person about whom no one at this point in time can say that it would ever be safe to release him again into society.
That is a very grave responsibility. It must be remembered that it is the cabinet which orders the sentence to be commuted. Therefore it is the cabinet which takes the responsibility of saying that this man will not be hanged but will be subject to life imprisonment. In view of the factors that I have outlined we have felt that it is not inappropriate that, in this particular and restricted class of case as it will be in the future, we should say, "The cabinet which orders the commutation shall also bear the final responsibility of determining whether that commutation will now result in his release in society".
In this process we, of course, shall have the benefit of the advice of the parole board. It is not as though we were going to set this man off in a corner where the parole board never saw him. They will have access to his file. They will review his case, and they will make recommendations. The situation simply is this. In that small segment of cases where there may be a real question whether it is ever going to be safe to release this man, we felt it to be appropriate that the cabinet which took the responsibility-not the same individuals but the governor in council-for determining that he should have his sentence of death commuted, should also have to bear the responsibility of deciding whether or not he will be released.
Let me impress upon my hon. friend this final point. This will not be the situation with regard to every case of commutation. This situation-I refer to the situation that the governor in council must finally authorize release-will apply only if at the time of making the commutation the governor in council so orders. In other words the governor in council at the time of authorizing the commutation must say that "in this particular case we think the case is so dangerous or so delicate or so border line that we now provide that he shall not be released on parole unless and until the cabinet authorizes it". May I also remind my hon. friend of another parallel. If in the course of a murder trial the jury were to find that the accused is insane, then the law provides that, instead of being sentenced to death, he shall be

ordered to be detained during the pleasure of the lieutenant-governor in council. In other words he is committed to an insane asylum until the lieutenant-governor in council decides that he is cured or is fit to be released. Then if the cabinet of Canada or the governor in council commutes a sentence because they feel this man is not mentally normal, under the law as it is at the present time there is no parallel authority to order that he be detained during the pleasure of the governor in council. Hence all we are doing is importing into the situation where we order a man detained because we have doubts as to his mental capacity, the same situation that prevails if the jury finds he is insane, in which case the sentence is that he be detained at the pleasure of the lieutenant-governor in council.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
As we come to
the end of the amendments I believe we are conscious of the fact that this particular subsection deals with the basic philosophy behind this measure in so far as government policy is concerned. The bill throughout, I think, represents an attempt at laudable compromise. I think the bill-and I have said this previously and I do not recall any comment being made about this by the minister-aims now to put into statute law a practice which quite legally and constitutionally has been exercised by the crown since this administration came into office in respect of the royal prerogative. One has the deep feeling that the considerations which have motivated the crown in Canada in the number of commutations that have taken place are to be found in the principles of this bill. There is nothing wrong and there is certainly no unconstitutional act involved in the crown seeking to put into the law of the land for administration and adjudication by the courts situations which have formed its basic policy in the consideration of how it would exercise the royal prerogative.
However, this clause raises a number of other considerations that were mentioned by the Prime Minister, and the contrast between what the Prime Minister said and what this clause provides cannot go unnoticed. It is time that in this particular the Prime Minister was speaking by way of obiter dictum and his remarks did not have the sanctity of any law, but they were the views of the head of the government and on that account must receive more than ordinary attention.
Before commenting on what the Prime Minister said I should remind hon. members of the committee that in this clause the instrument of commutation is provided not by members of the cabinet or by a committee 90205-6-373J
Criminal Code
of the cabinet but by the governor in council. It is the governor in council, and not members of the cabinet, who is charged with the responsibility of dealing at some subsequent time with the question of the extent of the accused's confinement.
The Prime Minister told us that these capital cases took a good deal of the cabinet's time. I am aware of that fact. I am aware, as one who sat in Her Majesty's privy council in Canada, that the cabinet of this country is obliged to give much time, and necessarily so as long as the authority is reposed with it, to the consideration of capital cases.
The Prime Minister went on to complain about, I should not say the length of time but undoubtedly, as head of the government with his preoccupations, he was placing on one side the many responsibilities and the many questions that have to be considered and on the other the time that is consumed by the cabinet as a whole in the consideration of capital cases. I suggest that as great a factor as that may be, the number of capital cases in this country are not so numerous as to cause any cabinet to feel that it could not properly discharge its role in the exercise of the royal prerogative.
The Prime Minister went on to remind us that in the United Kingdom the home secretary exercises the power of clemency or commutation without any reference whatsoever to his cabinet colleagues. Indeed I think the Prime Minister went on to say that he does not even discuss it with the lord chancellor. On that score there seems to be some doubt. In any event it is clear that in the United Kingdom the home secretary does not discuss the matter with his cabinet colleagues, except possibly the lord chancellor who is of course a member of the cabinet.
The Prime Minister went on to say that perhaps we might evolve a practice in Canada where the exercise of clemency could be left to the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General. I would simply point out that I think that would be a dangerous practice to evolve, in the light of the possible compromises because of this clause. In any event, that suggestion of the Prime Minister is not met in this clause because the role of recommending clemency and the ultimate role of determining the extent of confinement is to be exercised by the governor in council under this clause. I think that would have been the proper course for the Minister of Justice to have proposed.
It would seem to me to leave the decision in the first instance and in the ultimate instance to any body other than the governor in council, particularly at this time when this very important measure is about to be

Criminal Code
enacted, involving as it does a very important departure from our practice, would be a very dangerous procedure.
The hon. member for Vancouver East wondered why the question of confinement should go back to the cabinet in the first instance. I am satisfied with the validity of the reply made by the Minister of Justice. The minister says that the cabinet, having ordered the commutation, is to be the body that will order the accused to continue in confinement. As the minister pointed out, it will not necessarily be the same cabinet. That is not without some disability because, one cabinet having been seized with all the facts and having ordered commutation in the case of a person in respect of whom the sentence of death was commuted to life imprisonment, will not have the same freshness in the second consideration as the cabinet which had the responsibility for the original act.
Mr. Chairman, I think it is desirable and I strongly support the minister in saying that when we are making very important departures from the punishment of death in the case of wilful murder or, as it is called in the bill, capital murder planned or deliberate, we should make sure that in cases where the sentence of death has been commuted to life imprisonment the confinement is one that will protect the interests of society as well as providing for a proper measure of justice in so far as it is humanly possible to do that by human adjudication and by resorting to human standards.
I do not think there would be satisfaction in the country unless it were provided that the cabinet have the responsibility of reviewing recommendations made by the parole board as to the release of an accused person who had been sentenced to death for the crime of murder.
It may be that we will not always want these particular subclauses to stay on the statute books. It may be that the pressure of government business will make it difficult for a measure of this kind to prevail. Certainly when our country expands to a population twice its present size the problems of government will increase in consequence and so will the responsibilities of the cabinet. There may also be practical considerations and other reasons that will cause us to take a second look at this provision.
However, at this time I think the minister would not be meeting the wishes of most people in this country unless safeguards of this kind were provided. This means the cabinet is going to have put on it double the load about which the Prime Minister complained. If the cabinet now spends a considerable amount of time in considering what it should do in regard to capital cases, it is

now going to have to spend perhaps almost double that time in considering them.
I say this because if one bears in mind the record of commutations of this government one realizes the cabinet is going to have to spend a very considerable time in deciding whether or not a parole board's advice should be acted on and whether or not an individual sentenced to death, having had his sentence commuted to life imprisonment, is to be released as having fulfilled the life sentence substituted as a result of the commutation.
One wonders whether there will be the same care exercised by the cabinet with regard to the matter of further confinement or release from prison in the case of one who has been found guilty of murder, who has been sentenced to death but whose sentence has been commuted. Is the government going to take the same care in that direction as is taken with regard to the original act of commutation? I suspect there will be the same care, but I put the question in order to indicate the further burden which will be imposed on the cabinet and, I think, properly so, by this clause. The minister did say a moment ago that this bill does not in any way reduce the royal prerogative. I do not agree. I think this bill does reduce the incidence of the application of the royal prerogative just as the practice of commutation under this administration has resulted in an abridgement of the exercise of the royal prerogative by this particular cabinet executive as compared with its predecessor.
It seems to me that this is a compromise measure. I have expressed the view that although I do not agree with the draftsmanship of the bill it does meet my own point of view in principle. It obviously satisfies the government and it is likely a continuation of the practice which the government has itself pursued in considering how the royal prerogative shall be exercised. But it is a departure. The hon. member for Essex West said he voted for this bill on the assumption that we were retaining capital punishment. I have not read all the speeches made by those who participated in the debate on that subject but I do know that the private view of some members of this house is that through this measure we are taking a very forward step toward removing capital punishment altogether. That being the case, if we are going to be true to the opinions of those who have taken one position or another with regard to this bill it seems to me that this should be a trial measure only. We should resort to no process of finality in this legislation. We should adopt the procedure adopted in the United Kingdom of a five-year trial period-I think it was five years. I should like to see the minister say, without in any

way diluting or abridging the policy which the government has in mind, and without in any way retreating from the position it has taken, that in view of the importance of this matter to the administration of justice in this country the government proposes that this amendment should become law for a period of, let us say, five years or three years at the end of which time the amendment could be reviewed and the government of that day and the parliament of that day would come forward with new recommendations and urdertake a review of the position.
This suggestion does not in any way interfere with the principle of the bill and it would give many people in the country the feeling that in making this important departure we had acted in accordance with humanitarian instincts, in accordance with new concepts of the relation between offenders and the state and in accordance with new standards of morality while being, at the same time, moderate in our action and careful to keep within the rules of prudence. I think that is a consideration to which the minister might well give some attention and I hope he will say something about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Before dealing with the last suggestion made by the hon. member for Essex East may I comment on what he said about the remarks made by the Prime Minister in this house on May 29? I think the hon. gentleman has to some extent misinterpreted what the Prime Minister said. The Prime Minister in indicating his views as to the procedures that might be followed in cabinet was doing nothing more or less, as I apprehend him, than taking this house into his confidence, as is so typical of him, as to the ways in which he feels our procedures, even our cabinet procedures, might be improved. The hon. member for Essex East appeared to take from the Prime Minister's remarks the impression that the right hon. gentleman thought a small committee of cabinet should have the final decision. That is not correct. What the Prime Minister said was that he felt that with respect to cabinet procedures we might approach more closely the procedures in the United Kingdom. As reported at page 5528 of Hansard the words used were:
-whereby the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General would make a determination and recommendation and, on the basis of the opportunity now given to juries to recommend mercy, would be able to bring their recommendation to the cabinet as a whole.
It is clear from those words that the Prime Minister had no intention of suggesting that a small committee of cabinet should make the final decision in these matters and, as I have said, the Prime Minister was not in any
Criminal Code
way attempting to lay down a principle of law. All he did was to take the house into his confidence with respect to his thinking as to how procedures even in cabinet might be improved.
With regard to the proposal that there should be a five year test period-that we should announce as a government that we are not laying down any final rule but would be prepared to review the act at the end of five years-I appreciate the evident intention of the hon. member to prejudge events and I agree with him that undoubtedly this government will have the opportunity to review the measure in five years. We shall be here five years from now.
But it is not necessary for us to write into the statute an intention to review it in five years. After all, the law is a living thing. The law progresses, and if it is found that in spite of the collective judgment of the government, the House of Commons and the parliament of Canada this has not proved to be a wise and desirable amendment, then, of course, we would invite parliament to make further changes. However, I suggest with all respect to the hon. member that when you are dealing with the law affecting people's lives it is not a good thing to say: we intend to do this for five years to see if it works and if it does not we shall change it.
We believe this legislation is sound and progressive. We are convinced that it meets the wishes of the people of Canada and that it does more. Not only does it reflect public opinion but it reflects that standard of morality of conduct by which the public of Canada would wish, in the highest sense, to be governed. In that sense we submit this bill to the judgment of parliament, not in any inflexible sense, not in the sense of saying "We are doing this and we must be right", but in our firm belief that it is a proper course to take. If it should prove not to have been a wise move, we should be prepared to consider amending it, not in five years, but at any time it becomes apparent that changes should be considered. I do not believe that it would be appropriate to put a five year time limit on any legislation as important and, if I may say so, as well conceived as this which, as I anticipate, will receive that indication from the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the request of the committee, clause 1 was allowed to stand while we considered the possibility of amendments to take care of three suggestions. The first was that it should be made abundantly clear that a person who kills a police officer, or a member of a police force in the course of discharging the duties of that office, should be presumed to be guilty of capital murder. Second, that a person who kills a prison officer in the course of the discharging of his duties shall also be presumed to be guilty of capital murder. Third, the suggestion was made that the words used in the French version of this bill do not accurately reflect the English words in clause 1 (2)(a). The words involved are "planned and deliberate".
With regard to the first two of those suggestions, as I have indicated, it is our view that by virtue of the present draft, a person who kills a policeman in the execution of his duties, or a prison officer in the execution of his duties, would be guilty of capital murder as presently defined. However, as I indicated earlier, if there is doubt in this regard, in our readiness to be flexible, we are prepared to admit that we should not always have the last word, and are prepared to accept an amendment in order to clear away that doubt. Accordingly, I have had an amendment drafted which I will ask one of my colleagues to move after I have presented and explained its effect.
The first amendment would be made by striking out line 11 on page 1 and substituting therefor the word "person". Second, by striking out line 25 on page 1 and substituting the following:

Subparagraph (iv), or (c) such person by his own act caused or assisted in causing the death of (i) a police officer, police constable, constable, sheriff, deputy sheriff, sheriff's officer or other person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace acting in the course of his duties, or (ii) a warden, deputy warden, instructor, keeper, gaoler, guard or other officer or permanent employee of a prison, acting in the course of his duties, or counselled or procured another person to do any act causing or assisting in causing the death.

the second reading of Bill No. C-97, to amend an act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I explained at the time when leave to introduce the bill was given, the purpose of the bill is to provide for a further year a moratorium which was first provided in an amendment in 1959, which has the effect that certain activities of the fishing companies and fishing unions in British Columbia which might otherwise be found to be contraventions of the Combines Investigation Act shall be deemed for this period not to be contraventions. This is necessary because the restrictive trade practices commission now has before it a report of the director of investigation in which he alleges that these practices do raise questions under the Combines Investigation Act. However, the matter has not yet been settled, and if we were not to provide this moratorium the fishing industry in British Columbia would be thrown into considerable disorder.
The reason for the delay in settling the issue is that there have arisen certain side issues in the course of the hearings arranged by the restrictive trade practices commission which have been the subject of injunction applications which have unduly protracted those hearings. Therefore I am asking that this moratorium be extended for a further year, until December, 1962.

Combines Investigation Act

subtopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT AND CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF MORATORIUM RESPECTING B.C. FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the government ought to end this kind of farce here and now. The Combines Investigation Act was designed originally to protect consumers and the ordinary working people of our nation. However, inadvertently, I believe, a misuse is being made of this act. This is a deliberate attempt to smash a legitimate union of the fishermen, and they have been kept out on the limb now for a long time.
I can remember our present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) expressing his opinion of the Combines Investigation Act when he was in the opposition ranks. He called for an act that had some teeth in it and for confinement behind bars of those who were found guilty of violating the intent of the act. I am sure that it never was the intent of the act to prevent the working people of Canada from combining with one another to get a fair deal. Yet, by one means or another, over a period of many years now, under both Liberal and Conservative governments, our fishermen have had a gun pointed at their heads. I believe it is high time that the government came clean and discontinued this particular investigation or demanded that the fishing companies produce their own records.
It is very easy. Mr. Speaker, to ask a fisherman to produce his records. These records are a matter of public knowledge. Yet, under the leadership of a former minister of the crown, the fishing companies are holding a gun at the head of the fishermen in British Columbia. This investigation is resented very deeply by all the working people of British Columbia, and we appeal to the government to end this nonsense once and for all. Either bring the fishing companies to task, make them open their books and expose their nefarious dealings to the public or allow the union of fishermen to negotiate as they have in the past in the interests of all our fishermen.

Mr. Speaker, last year we were bitterly critical of various sections of the combines bill which was then before us. This year, we still have some fears about the way in which the act is administered. The rather simple amendment now before the house, providing for a one year extension of certain privileges granted to fishermen in British Columbia, prompts me to ask this question: Do the fishermen of the rest of Canada not have the same rights as the fishermen of British Columbia?
I know that in the fishing industry, it is often very hard to sell at prices that will

enable the fishermen to earn a decent living. If the purpose of this bill is to help needy fishermen, I am quite prepared to support it. On the other hand, if this is true for one part of the country, it must also be true for the rest of the country. Those who fish on the Atlantic coast must be in a similar situation and should enjoy equal privileges.
I am therefore wondering, as was mentioned a moment ago by the hon. member for Coquitlam (Mr. Regier)-I forget the exact name of his constituency-Burnaby-Coquitlam, I think-

I will not say it is like a revolver placed at the back of the head of a certain class of citizens, but I will say that if this is needed -and this must be proven-in one section of the country, it should also be needed in the rest of the country, because the plight of fishermen is serious throughout Canada, and there should be protection both for the Atlantic fishermen and the Pacific fishermen.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one of those bills which are becoming perennial and each time it is presented the minister is asked to make it applicable across the country, as the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) has just suggested, or the minister is asked to make the moratorium effective for a sufficiently long period of time to encompass all of the activities that are going on in the fishing industry of British Columbia because that is what the bill deals with.
The reason that the bill is before us arises from the fact that an inquiry was initiated consequent upon the statement of six citizens five or six years ago, and it is one of the very few inquiries that have been initiated in this way. In general the inquiry dealt

with a price conspiracy in the fishing industry of British Columbia primarily with regard to sales on the export market. Last year there was an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act which provided that it was all right to engage in what we would call illegal conspiracies so far as the export field is concerned, and no sooner was the bill passed than the fisheries association of British Columbia issued a statement that parliament had now agreed that it had been proper for the fishing companies to engage in price conspiracies in past years. This, of course, is quite untrue.
The point is that by a series of legal manoeuvres involving applications for injunctions and so on-I understand the matter is now before the courts so perhaps we should not debate it too much-the inquiry that was started some five or six years ago has not even reached the stage of the restrictive trade practices commission holding hearings and the commission has not even progressed halfway toward making a report on its findings.
Like the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam (Mr. Regier), I think the situation is becoming more farcical all the time. I for one believe that when the Combines Investigation Act was amended by parliament last session the minister should have introduced amendments to those sections of the act which state in essence that it shall not apply to workmen who combine for their own protection, or whatever the phraseology is, to ensure that this sort of legal persecution was discontinued. As I say, this is one of those types of bills that are becoming perennial. We find ourselves in the position of not being able to do anything at the moment other than support it and in effect allow these associations to engage again in illegal activities with the sanction of a statute until the matter is cleared up. But I think it is a disgrace that delaying tactics of this sort can go on year after year and that parliament should find itself in the position of having to provide moratorium after moratorium year after year to allow the situation to continue. I wonder whether I might call it 10.30, Mr. Speaker?
